client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I'm glad you did. How have things been since we last spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... my sister basically guilted me into it, so. I don't know why I'm here, honestly. Nothing's really changed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even being guilted into something — you still made the choice to walk through that door again. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. It's just... been a rough week. The apartment's quiet and I — I don't know. It is what it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that quiet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The drinking helps. I know that's what you want to talk about, but... it's the only time I don't sit there thinking about everything I lost. Everything I — yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The alcohol gives you some relief from the grief. Like a pause button on all of that loss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. She took the kids, you know? Every other weekend now. I used to coach my son's soccer team. Every Saturday. Now I'm just — sitting in a two-bedroom apartment watching ESPN by myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like, when you let yourself think about that? About your son, the soccer field?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... hard. I get angry, mostly. At her. Because she's the one who—

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I wasn't around enough either. I worked a lot. I thought that was — I thought that's what I was supposed to do. Provide. And now my kids barely call and I just... what was the point of any of it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's real doubt starting to surface alongside the anger. A wondering about your own part in things. And then that question — what was the point — when that hits you late at night, what does that feel like in your body?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrifying, honestly. Like... I'm 48. And I'm starting over? What if I can't — what if they don't need me anymore? My kids.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fear that you might lose them — not legally, but really lose them, their closeness — that's sitting right underneath everything else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to be that dad who becomes a stranger. I've seen that happen to guys. Their kids grow up and the dad is just... some guy who shows up at Christmas and doesn't know anything about their lives.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to say back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You've been using alcohol to get through nights that feel unbearable. The anger at your ex is real — but underneath it there's grief. About the life you thought you were building. About missing your son on that soccer field. And underneath all of that is this fear — that if things keep going the way they're going, you could really lose your kids. Not to a court order, but to distance. And that one... that's the thing that scares you most.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I... yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. [long pause] I hadn't really put it together like that before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you look ahead — past the anger, past the apartment, past all of this — what matters most to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My kids. That's the obvious answer, but it's true. I want them to respect me. I want my son to look back someday and think — his dad handled this. Like, handled it like a man. Not like someone who just fell apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being the kind of father your son can look up to — that still lives in you. Even now. Maybe especially now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I know — I know the drinking isn't helping that. I'm not stupid about it. I just... I don't know what to do with all of it otherwise. The evenings are the worst part.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you don't know what to do with it otherwise. What have you tried, even small things, when it gets bad?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I called my buddy Dave once when it got really bad. Just to talk. That... that actually helped, weirdly. But I felt stupid about it after. Like I shouldn't need that at my age.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Calling Dave — that took something. Reaching out when you're hurting and part of you is saying you should be able to handle this alone — that's not weakness. That's actually one of the things that keeps men connected to their lives, to the people who matter.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Huh. I never... my dad was not a feelings kind of guy, so. [small laugh] I always thought asking for help meant something was wrong with you. Maybe I can call Dave more. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — even something small — over the next week or two, to take one step toward the father you want to be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could reach out to my son. Just text him. I've been waiting for him to reach out first, but maybe that's not fair — he's sixteen. I'm the adult. And maybe... I don't know, actually deal with the drinking. Like actually talk to someone about it. Which I guess is sort of what this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back this week. You let yourself sit with something really painful today — the grief underneath the anger, the fear underneath that. You named what you're afraid of losing, and what still matters to you. And now you're talking about texting your son tonight and being honest with yourself about the drinking. That's real movement. I don't want to rush past how hard this has been. But I don't think you came back here today because you'd given up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I haven't. [pause] I'll text him tonight.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I know you said you're pressed for time — there's no pressure here. Sit wherever feels comfortable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... I've got like twenty minutes, maybe less. I don't even really know why I'm here. My manager basically said I had to come or it would go on my record or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So someone told you that you had to be here. That's a tough spot. What's your sense of... what they think this is about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — okay, so I came into my shift one morning and I guess I was still kind of... I hadn't slept great. And I dropped a tray. Like one tray. And my manager acted like I showed up drunk or something, which is — that's not what happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want me to know it wasn't what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because it wasn't. It was a Sunday morning shift, okay? I'd been out with friends the night before, I didn't sleep enough. That's — every college student does that. That's not a problem, that's just... that's college.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And this is happening in the same stretch of time where your friends sat you down too, from what I understand. What was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That was... okay that was weird. And honestly kind of embarrassing? Like they made it into this whole thing, like an intervention, like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It was a lot. I felt like I was on a reality show or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds really jarring. People you trust, sitting around you, saying things you didn't expect to hear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They don't even — like, they drink too. Every single one of them. Jake literally can't watch a football game without a six-pack. So I don't get why I'm the one sitting here. It's hypocritical, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still showed up though. Feeling all of that — the embarrassment, the frustration — you still walked through that door today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I kind of had to. For my job. It wasn't like — I don't want you to think I'm here because I agree with any of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear that. I'm not trying to talk you into anything. I'm just wondering — your friends, your manager... what do you think they're actually seeing that has them this worried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I genuinely don't know. I think they're overreacting. Yes, I drink on weekends, that's what people do senior year. You work hard all week and then you let loose. I'm not, like, drinking during class or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your friends pulled you aside. Your manager wrote you up. And you're here telling me everyone's overreacting. That's... a lot of people, in a pretty short window of time, all pointing in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well — maybe they all need to mind their own business. Seriously. I'm twenty-one, I'm legal, I'm not hurting anyone. What I do on a Friday night has nothing to do with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just... sit with what I'm hearing for a second. You came in rushed, feeling like you were forced here. You had something happen at work that you feel got completely blown out of proportion. Your friends did something that felt humiliating, even if they care about you. And underneath all of it, there's this message that keeps finding you — people are worried. ...

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I mean. Yeah. I guess that's... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is there any part of this — even a small part — that you wonder about yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... sometimes I wake up and I don't really remember everything from the night before. And that's — I used to think that was just funny. Like a good story to tell. But lately it's been happening more and I'm like... huh. But that still doesn't — that doesn't mean I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It used to feel like a funny story. Now it's starting to feel like something else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Maybe. I don't know. I haven't really said that out loud before. It's like — I don't want to make it a big thing because then it becomes a big thing. You know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — a year from now, five years from now — if nothing changed at all?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, I've actually thought about that. I'm graduating in May and I'm supposed to start this job in the city and I just — I don't want to be that guy, you know? The one who peaked in college and couldn't hold it together. My dad's kind of like that and I've always said I wouldn't be...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know exactly who you don't want to become. And that matters to you — really deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess it does. I'm not my dad, I'm not — I'm not saying I'm him. But I also don't want to wake up one day and realize I missed the window where I could've actually done something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a part of you that's already watching ahead — looking for that moment before it gets too far. That part of you showed up here today even when the rest of you didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came in here thinking this was going to be stupid. Like a box to check. And I still — I mean, I'm still not calling myself an alcoholic or whatever. But I'm not... I'm not totally comfortable with where things are either. That's a weird thing to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to have it all figured out today. But I'm wondering — is there one thing, even something really small, that you'd be willing to try? Just to see what it feels like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... maybe just keeping track. Like actually noticing how much I'm drinking instead of just going along with it. Not stopping — I'm not ready for — I'm not saying I'll stop. But maybe just... paying attention. I could probably do that.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So... it's good to see you here today. I know it's been a rough few days. Before we get into anything, I just want to check in — how are you doing right now, sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here, right? [sighs] I don't really want to be but... whatever. My mom basically dropped me off. Said she wasn't gonna leave until I walked through the door.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your mom made sure you got here. [pause] That sounds like she was pretty shaken up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She cried the whole drive over. Which — I mean, I'm fine. I woke up in the ER with a monitor on my finger and some nurse asking me if I knew what day it was and I was... it was embarrassing, okay? But I'm fine now. I don't know why everyone's making it into this huge thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You woke up not knowing where you were, with your mom crying. What was going through your mind in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I was pissed off. Like — it wasn't even that serious. My buddies just... they called 911 because I passed out at a party. That happens. People pass out at parties all the time. It doesn't require the whole... [waves hand] production.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you was angry that people made a big deal out of it. And I'm also hearing something underneath that — maybe some embarrassment too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... [long pause] Yeah. My girlfriend was there. She... she hasn't texted me since. So. That's great. Really great. [laughs bitterly] But I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The people who matter most — your girlfriend, your mom — they're both pulling back right now. That's a painful place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, man. I don't know what they want from me. Like I stopped going out for three weeks after the whole intervention thing and what changed? Nothing. My grades are still trash. My girlfriend was barely talking to me anyway. So what's the point. What's even the point of any of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You tried pulling back for a while and things still didn't get better, and now you're sitting here wondering if any of this even matters. That sounds exhausting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been coming here for like two months. I'm supposed to be making progress or whatever. But then this weekend happens and I'm right back to square one. Maybe I'm just... maybe some people just can't change. Like maybe that's just how it is for certain people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to come back to that idea — that maybe you can't change. But I want to name something first. You have shown up here, consistently, for two months. Even today, after everything. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't even know why I bother. [pause] Like, I showed up because I had to, or because... I don't even know. It doesn't feel like it's doing anything. I just feel... I don't know. Empty.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say empty — can you tell me more about what that feels like? What does empty mean for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... nothing feels good anymore. Even when I'm drinking it's not like it used to be. It used to just be fun, you know? Now I'm just doing it because... something to do. And then it goes sideways and I end up in a hospital bed and my mom's crying and I'm still sitting here telling you I'm fine like some kind of idiot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So even the drinking itself — it's not giving you what it used to. You're still doing it, but it's not filling anything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess. [pause] I don't know. I just... senior year was supposed to be the best year. That's what everyone says. And instead I'm... this. Whatever this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Senior year was supposed to mean something to you. You had a picture of what it was going to look like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wanted to like... I had this idea I'd be graduating, have a job lined up, maybe things with me and Kayla would be... [trails off] I'm supposed to graduate in six weeks. I haven't applied to a single job. Not one. I've just been too busy... surviving, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still have that image — graduation, a job, things working out with Kayla. That vision isn't gone, even after everything that happened this weekend.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess I still care about that stuff. [pause] I just don't know how to get there from here. Like the gap between where I am and where I want to be feels... massive. Like I'm looking at it across a canyon or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You care about graduating. You care about Kayla. You care about having a future that means something. That caring — it's still there. Even after a weekend that knocked you completely down.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. [long pause] Yeah, I do care. I'm not — I'm not giving up or whatever. I just... I got scared this weekend. Like actually scared. When the nurse read off my blood alcohol level I was like... that can't be right. That number cannot be right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when you heard that number. What was the feeling in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... reality just hitting me in the face, maybe. My friend Jake, he looked it up on his phone right there in the waiting room and showed me and he had this look — like he didn't know who I was anymore. And I... that hit me. That really hit me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing across this whole conversation. You came in today because you had to. You were angry, you felt like nothing was working, like you couldn't change. And underneath all of that — you're scared. You're grieving the senior year you wanted. And there was a moment in that hospital, when you saw that number and saw Jake's face, when something real cracked through. You still have the things you care about. You're still here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet] Yeah. I mean... I don't know what I'm doing next. But I guess I'm here. And I guess that's... I don't know. Maybe that's something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is something. Showing up when everything in you said don't — that matters. So given everything you just told me... what feels like one thing, even something small, that you could hold onto this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I don't know, maybe I text Kayla. Not like trying to fix everything, just like... check in. And maybe I look at one job posting. Just one. I'm not promising anything but... maybe just that.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know getting here after everything you've been through — that's not a small thing. This is a space where you can be honest. No agenda, no judgment. How are you feeling right now, walking in that door?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... fine. I mean, I don't really know why I'm here, honestly. The hospital said I should come, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The hospital said you should come. What's your take on that — do you think they had a point, or does it feel more like something you got pushed into?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think they were overreacting, personally. I just... I hadn't eaten much, and the drinks hit me harder than usual. It wasn't like I was trying to — it wasn't what they made it sound like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you're sitting, this was more of a one-time thing. A bad night. Not necessarily part of a bigger pattern.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I mean, I've been drinking more since Gerald died, obviously. Anyone would. But I'm not — I don't have a problem. I just needed something to take the edge off. Eight months, and people act like I should be over it already.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Eight months since Gerald died. Tell me more about what those eight months have actually looked like for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do they look like? They look like... like nothing, really. I get up. I try to get through the day. The house is so quiet. I used to hate quiet and now I just — the drinking, it fills in the quiet a little. I'm not hurting anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying something enormous — losing Gerald, losing the life you two had together — and you found a way to keep getting up every day. That took real endurance, even if the way you've been coping has also come at a cost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'd call it endurance. I just... didn't have much choice, did I? And I know the drinking is — I know it's not ideal. But it's been manageable. Or it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'it was.' What changed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The ER was scary. Waking up there, not being totally sure how I got there. And it was me who called 911 — which means some part of me knew something was wrong, and I still can't quite... I've never been in a hospital that way before. Not as the patient.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you knew something was wrong. Even in the middle of it, some part of you reached out. That part was trying to protect you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I keep thinking Gerald would be — he'd be so worried if he could see me. He took such good care of me for thirty-one years. And now I'm ending up in emergency rooms alone. That's not... that's not who I want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Who do you want to be? What does that look like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone my kids aren't scared for, I think. My daughter called me twice that night and I didn't pick up. I couldn't face her. She's worried sick and I just... I keep pushing people away. I don't really know why I do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're pushing people away, and a part of you is watching yourself do it, and it's starting to bother you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. I mean... I used to be the person everyone called. I'd show up with a casserole when someone was sick, I'd be the first one there. Now I don't answer my own daughter's calls. Something has gone very wrong somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean — for you, in your bones — to get back to being that person? The one who shows up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean... I'd have to actually feel things again. And that terrifies me. Because if I stop numbing it, then Gerald is really gone. Like, really gone. The grief is just waiting for me on the other side of all this. Does that make any sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. The drinking has been keeping the full weight of losing him at arm's length. And there's a part of you that's afraid if you let go of that buffer, the grief will be unbearable. That it'll swallow you whole.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly that. And I know it sounds crazy, to prefer... I know it's not actually keeping me safe. I know that. I just haven't known what else to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You lost Gerald eight months ago, and drinking became a way to survive the silence, to keep the worst of the pain just far enough away to function. Then the ER happened. You called 911 yourself. You're sitting here today. You're thinking about your daughter, about the kind of woman you used to be. There's a part of you that is clearly not okay with where things have gone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not okay with it. I haven't been okay with it for a while, I think. I just... didn't let myself look at it until now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of honesty — being able to look at it and actually name it — that's harder than it sounds. A lot of people can't get there. The fact that you can, that matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I cried every single day for the first three months after he died. Every day. And then I just... stopped. And I think the drinking got worse right around then. Like I was patching over something. Maybe I need to go back and — and actually cry some more. [small, wet laugh] God, listen to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it feel like to actually do that — to grieve him all the way through, with some real support around you instead of doing it alone in a quiet house?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like being scraped open, probably. But also maybe... maybe like actually getting somewhere. I've just been treading water for so long. I am so tired. I'm tired of being this version of me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Then I want you to hear this clearly: you are exhausted from carrying this alone. You are scared to feel the grief, but you're also scared of what happens if you keep not feeling it. You want to be someone your daughter doesn't have to worry about. And the part of you that called 911 and walked in here today — that part is already fighting for you. That is exactly where we start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Yeah... I'd like to figure out how to do that. I don't want to keep living like this. Gerald wouldn't have wanted this for me. I know that. I've always known that.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making the time today — I know you mentioned you're between classes. Before we get into anything, I just want you to know this is an open conversation. There's no agenda I'm trying to push. So, welcome.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... honestly I'm not even sure why I'm here. The person who referred me basically said I should come talk to someone. I've got like 45 minutes before I have to be back, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here partly because someone suggested it. What's your own take on that — what do you think they were concerned about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, a colleague — she noticed I seemed off one morning and made it into... I don't know, a whole thing. I had a rough night, I wasn't feeling great. That happens to people. That happens to everyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from your perspective, it was one rough morning, and it got blown out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like, I've been teaching for eleven years. I'm good at my job, my students — I mean, I care about those kids. One bad day and suddenly there's this whole... concern about me. It's a little insulting, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You clearly take your work seriously. Can you tell me a little bit about what evenings look like for you, typically, after school?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I unwind. I pour a drink when I get home, watch something, decompress. Teaching middle school is — I don't know if you've spent time around 13-year-olds, but it's a lot. You need to come down somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Finding ways to decompress after a job like that is something most people need — that makes complete sense. When you say you pour a drink, what does that usually look like over the course of a whole evening?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Three, maybe four drinks. Sometimes more if it's been a bad day. Wine mostly. Sometimes whiskey. I'm not like... chugging it. It's spread out over a few hours.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And on those mornings after — what's that experience like, getting up and heading in to school?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's fine, usually. Sometimes I'm a little foggy. I drink a lot of coffee. I mean... the morning that Sarah noticed, that was worse than usual. I'll give her that much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So most mornings you manage, but there are times — like that one — where it's harder to shake. And it sounds like part of you can see why she might have been worried.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't say I think she was right to go report it or whatever she did. I just said that morning was rough. That's — look, everyone has bad days. I'm not an alcoholic. I want to be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing so far, make sure I've got it right. You came in today because someone expressed concern, and it feels overblown to you — what she saw was an exception. At the same time, you're describing drinking most evenings, sometimes pretty significantly, and occasional mornings where you're not fully yourself. And you're clear you don't see this as a real problem. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds worse than it is. I... yeah, that's the rough outline. But context matters. I'm under a lot of pressure right now. This isn't just about the drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned pressure — what's going on for you outside of school? What's life been like lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My... my dad got sick last year. He's in a care facility now. My marriage has been — it's not great. My wife thinks I drink too much too, so. She's been saying that for a while. But I've got everything under control. I'm still functioning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot right now. A sick parent, a marriage that's strained, a demanding job — and the drinking has become a way to get through it. And the two people in your life who noticed, your wife and your colleague, they're not comparing notes. They got there separately.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I... hm. I haven't really — I've been telling myself Diane's just been on my case because things have been tense between us. But Sarah at work, she's not... she doesn't stick her nose into people's business. That's not who she is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you that two people who don't really know each other noticed the same thing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... maybe I've been more obvious than I thought. And that bothers me. I don't want my students seeing me like that. That's not — I take that part seriously. That's the part that actually gets to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That says something real about you — that your first thought goes to your students. That's not a small thing. That's a value you're pointing to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been doing this long enough to know that some of those kids don't have a lot of stability at home. I'm supposed to be the steady person in the room. And lately I wonder if I've been that. I... I haven't wanted to look at that question too directly, I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you did let yourself look at it — what would you want to be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want to not feel like I need it every night. Like... I want to have a Tuesday where I just don't think about it. I used to be able to do that. I don't remember exactly when that changed. I'd like to feel more like myself again — like the version of me that had things more together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull this together before we wrap up. You came in today feeling a bit put on the spot, not sure any of this was necessary. But as we've talked, you've named some real pressures — your dad, your marriage, the job. You've acknowledged that two people who care about you noticed something you've been working hard not to look at yourself. And underneath all of that, there's this: you want to be the steady person in the room for your students. You miss feeling like yourself. That's not the picture of someone who doesn't care.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah. I came in ready to defend myself and I don't think I did a very good job of that. Which is maybe telling me something. I don't know what comes next, but I'm — I'm more open to figuring that out than I was an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That shift matters — even if it's just a crack in the door. Before you head back, what's one small thing you'd be willing to actually pay attention to between now and when we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... noticing. Like actually paying attention to how many nights I pour that drink on autopilot without even deciding to. Just — noticing. I think I can probably do that much.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — I'm Marcus, just call me Marcus. So before we do any of the official stuff, I gotta ask: what's it actually like being here today? Because the look on your face when you walked in was... something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, yeah. I mean, my doctor basically said I had to come. So... here I am. I've done this before, sat in these rooms, and it never really went anywhere. So I'm not exactly, like, pumped about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's less 'I woke up excited to talk to a counselor' and more 'my doctor made me do it and I've been burned before.'

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah, pretty much. I mean, I get why she flagged it, whatever. But the last few times I did this, it was always the same — worksheets, the same questions, I'd say the stuff I was supposed to say, and then I'd leave and nothing changed. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Going through the motions and walking out feeling like you wasted your time — that sounds genuinely exhausting. What do you think made it not stick those other times?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there for myself, I guess. Someone else wanted me to go. So I showed up and I'd say the right things and... I don't know, I figured that's just kind of how it goes with this stuff. You go, nothing happens, you move on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Actually, that's a real thing to notice about yourself — that you knew you were going through the motions, that you weren't actually buying in. A lot of people don't have that kind of read on themselves.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... sure. But honestly? I'm not even sure this time is different. My doctor sees one number on some screening and now I'm an alcoholic. I'm a bartender. I'm literally around alcohol all day. That's my job. That's my whole world.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The label feels completely off given your context — like she just ran a number without thinking about who you actually are or what your life looks like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not drinking on the job, okay? I drink after my shift. To come down. Every bartender I know does that — you work a six-hour rush, you're wired, you need something to decompress. That's just... that's just how it works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So within that world — late nights, the rush, winding down — where do you think the line actually is? Like what would it look like to you if someone in your world had a real problem?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I guess if it was messing stuff up. Work, relationships, whatever. But mine's not. I show up, I do my job, my girlfriend's not on my case about it. So like... what's the actual problem here?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those are the markers you'd use — showing up, job's fine, relationship's okay. And by those you're checking the boxes. ...You ran through that list pretty fast though.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Just that — you had that list ready to go real quick. And I'm curious, if things were genuinely fine, would you need to run the checklist? What's underneath that for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I don't know. I mean... okay, there's this thing that's been kind of sitting with me. I tried to think of the last time I didn't drink. Like, just one day. And I... I couldn't. I actually sat there and tried to come up with one day and I couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one landed on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It did. I kind of brushed it off at first but... that's not normal, right? Like even just — one day. I couldn't name one. That's... I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't just rationalize that away. A lot of people would have. You let yourself actually sit with it — that says something real about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been kind of... avoiding thinking about it too hard. Because I think if I look at it too closely I'm not gonna like what I see.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think you'd see?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who... uses it as a crutch, maybe. Like it's not really winding down anymore. It's more like — I don't feel right without it. Like something's off if I don't have it. And I... I don't like saying that out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It shifted from something you chose to something that feels more automatic. Less 'I want a drink' and more 'I need one to feel like myself.'

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... more accurate than I want it to be. I used to actually enjoy it, you know? Now I just — do it. Half the time I'm not even tasting it. I'm just going through the motions again, basically.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm getting this right. You came in today feeling pretty dragged here, done this before and it went nowhere, and you've been holding onto this idea that it all makes sense given your job and your world. But there's this other thing you've been quietly carrying — you can't name a sober day, and when you actually look at it, it doesn't feel like a choice anymore. And you're not even enjoying it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it all out there like that... yeah. That's a lot. That's kind of a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you that it's a lot?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I've been telling myself a story. That it's fine, it's the job, it's what bartenders do. And maybe some of that's even true, I don't know. But I think I've also been using that story to just... not look at this thing. And I don't know what to do with that yet, but I think — yeah. I think I've been hiding behind it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not sure what comes next. But you're also not looking away from it anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I'm not. That's... weird to say. But no. I'm not.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for logging on today. I know... setting up a video call for something like this isn't exactly how most people want to spend their afternoon. I'm glad you made it. Is where you are private enough? You've got some space?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm alone. Look, I'm just gonna say it right upfront — I don't want to be here. My lawyer basically told me I had to do this or I'd lose my license, maybe worse. So I'm here. But I'm not happy about it. At all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because you felt like you didn't really have a choice. And that... that's a genuinely frustrating position to be in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Frustrating doesn't even cover it. I'm furious. The whole thing is bull— I mean, look, I've been driving for twenty years. Twenty years. And one cop decides he doesn't like the look of me and suddenly I'm some kind of criminal? It's a joke.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you felt singled out. Can I ask... what's your take on what happened? Like from your perspective — how did you end up here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My take? I had a couple drinks at my buddy's place, I drove home — it was maybe a mile and a half — and this cop was just sitting there. Waiting. And my number came up. That's it. That's the whole story. But because it's my second one, they acted like I'm some raging alcoholic. I wasn't even drunk.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The way the system came down on you felt completely out of proportion to what you actually did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. A mile and a half. I've seen people way worse than me on the road. Way worse. But they didn't get caught, so they're fine. I got caught twice so now I'm — what — a danger to society? It's insane. The whole system is just... it's not about safety, it's about money.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know... whatever brought you here, you did show up today. That says something. A lot of people in your position just don't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I showed up because I had to. Don't read into it. I'm not — I'm not here because I think I have some problem. I'm here because a judge told me to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. So if you had to say — what would you actually want to walk away from these sessions with? Like if there's any version of this that doesn't feel like a complete waste of your time, what would that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Just getting through it. Check the boxes, get my license back, move on with my life. I've got a lot of stuff going on right now. I don't need this on top of everything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot on your plate right now. This is just... one more thing added to a pile that's already really heavy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. And look — I'm not trying to be a jerk to you personally. I just... I've got work stuff, and now this whole court thing, the fines, the fees... do you know how much this is costing me? For something I didn't even think was that serious. It's just — it's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's going on at work, if you don't mind me asking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We're going through layoffs. I've been there seven years and they're just cutting people left and right. I'm probably fine but... you don't know. You don't know until you know. And my ex has been dragging me back into court over custody stuff again so — yeah. It's just been a rough stretch. Like a really rough few months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seven years at a job, not knowing if you're safe. Custody battles on top of that. That's genuinely a lot to carry at once. It makes sense you're running on empty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. It has been rough. But — and I want to be clear about this — the drinking thing, that's not my issue. I drink like any other guy. I have a beer after work, a few on the weekend. Normal stuff. It's not like I'm sitting at home alone getting hammered every night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And I'm not here to tell you what you are or aren't. I'm just curious — with all that stress building up over this past year, has your drinking shifted at all? Like when you look back at it honestly?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe a little more than usual. Things have been stressful. I'm not gonna pretend they haven't. But that's just — that's what happens. Lots of people drink more when things are hard. When things calm down it goes back to normal. That's always how it's been for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I really appreciate you being straight with me about that. Given how this conversation started, that took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean, I'm not trying to lie to you. I just — I don't want to be put in a box. That word, alcoholic, it gets thrown around and it doesn't... it doesn't fit. That's not who I am. I've got a job, I've got kids, I function. I'm not some guy who can't get off the couch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm getting this right. You've had a genuinely brutal stretch — pressure at work, custody stuff, financial stress from all of this legal mess. You've been drinking a bit more than usual to cope, and you can see that. But you don't see yourself as someone with a drinking problem, and you're worried that label is going to get slapped on you when it doesn't fit. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. I got caught. Twice. And now everything is on the line and I'm sitting here on a video call talking to a therapist when I should be at work. That's — that's just where I'm at.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you. What would it look like for you if things actually started turning around — the custody situation, the job anxiety, just... the weight of all of it? What does a better version of the next year look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Getting my kids back on a regular schedule. That's... that's the main one. I miss them. And keeping my job. And just not having all this crap hanging over me all the time. I'm tired of fighting everything. Every single thing is a fight right now and I'm just... I'm exhausted, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to get back to your kids. You want things to feel steadier. And you're tired — really tired — of everything being such a struggle.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I am. I didn't really expect to say that today but. Yeah. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today pretty angry, and honestly that made a lot of sense given everything. And somewhere in the middle of all of it you shared some things that clearly matter a great deal to you. That's not nothing. I'm just wondering — is there any part of you that might be open to just... looking at some of this together over the next few sessions? No labels. No agenda. Just seeing what's actually there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe. I'm not making any promises. But... yeah, I'm not going anywhere I guess. So. Maybe.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — make yourself comfortable. I'm really glad you're here. I know finishing detox and then walking straight into a session is a lot to take on. I like to start by just checking in. How are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, yeah. I'm... okay, actually. Which is kind of weird to say? Like I figured I'd walk in here and be a total mess, but I think I'm just — I don't know, I made it through the detox and I just want to, like, keep going. So. Yeah. I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came through something really hard and you want to keep that momentum going. I'd like to understand more about what you're hoping for. What would make coming here today feel worthwhile to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly, I just... I want to understand why I got to the point where I couldn't remember the last time I was sober. Like, that freaked me out when I actually said it out loud to my friend. I've been pouring drinks for other people for five years and somehow I just... became one of the people I used to joke about, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment of hearing yourself say it out loud — that it had been so long you couldn't even remember — that landed differently than just thinking it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And I mean, I've been telling myself it's normal because of the job — like everyone in the industry drinks, right? But lately I've been thinking, okay, but do they all drink like *me*? And I don't know the answer to that. And that's kind of... that's a little scary.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'drink like me' — what does that actually look like, on a typical day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So I close most nights. We're talking midnight, one AM. And there's this whole winding-down thing, right? You have a shot with the crew after close, it's just how it's done. But then I'd go home and have a few more. And then on my days off I'd start earlier. I just — I didn't think about it as a schedule, but now looking back it kind of was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there was a structure to it — a routine built around drinking — that you didn't even see as a routine until you stepped back from it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And the detox doctor, she mentioned physical dependence? And I just — I didn't think that applied to me. I thought that was like, guys who drink in the morning and can't function. But apparently I was physically dependent and just... didn't know. That's the part that's hard to wrap my head around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a genuinely disorienting thing to find out about yourself. I'm curious — you've mentioned your job a few times now. How does the idea of changing your relationship with alcohol fit with still being a bartender?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's the thing, right? It's my whole life. Like, I'm actually good at what I do. I know my regulars, I know the craft, I genuinely love making cocktails. I'm not about to go work at a bank or whatever. But everyone's gonna know. My coworkers, my regulars... it's gonna be awkward. And I guess part of me is just — I don't know, pissed off that I even have to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built something real in that job. Real skill, real connections. And you're not willing to just walk away from that — that kind of clarity about what matters to you is actually important.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I just... I wasn't expecting to feel angry about it. I thought I'd come in here and be like, okay, fix me, let's go. But it's more complicated than that, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It usually is. And I think that anger makes complete sense — there's a real loss here. What has drinking actually taken from you, beyond just the physical stuff?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My memory, for one. The last year and a half is kind of blurry. Like I know things happened — my sister's birthday, my buddy's wedding — but I couldn't tell you details. And I think I've been checked out emotionally. My mom called me out on it a few months ago. Said I seemed 'far away' all the time. I brushed it off but... she was right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's real grief in what you're describing. A year and a half of your own life that you can't fully access. The people who love you noticing that you were gone even when you were standing right there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah. And that one's hard. Because I'm not a bad person, you know? Like I never thought of myself as someone who just disappears on people who matter to me. But I did. I kind of did do that. And I don't know how to... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in today with real momentum — you got through detox, you want to keep going. You started to see a pattern that you hadn't let yourself see before, and the physical dependence piece genuinely blindsided you. There's a part of you that's angry because your identity and your livelihood are all tangled up in this. And underneath that, there's grief — for time lost, for moments you can't remember, for being 'far away' from the people you love. That's a lot to be holding at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it all together like that... yeah. I think I've been dealing with each piece separately and not seeing that it's all the same thing. Like I kept compartmentalizing — this is the work stuff, this is the family stuff. But it's all just... it's all the alcohol stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really significant thing to see. If you picture yourself a year from now — having done this work — what does life look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Clearer. Like, just... clearer. I want to remember things. I want to show up to my sister's next birthday and actually be there, not just physically present. And honestly? I think I'd be a better bartender. Like, actually present with my customers instead of just running on autopilot. I don't know, maybe that sounds naive.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound naive at all. It sounds like you already know what you're working toward. Present. Actually there — not just going through the motions.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I think that's why the intervention hit me the way it did. My friend — he didn't come at me like 'you have a problem, you need help.' He just said, 'I miss you, man.' And that was it. That was enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: On a scale of one to ten, how confident are you right now that you can actually make this change stick?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hmm. Maybe a six? Like, I believe I can do it, but I don't know what I don't know yet. The detox was controlled. Out there it's my whole environment. But a six is more than I expected to feel walking in today, so... I'll take it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A six is real — that's something we can build on. Can I share something with you, just some information? A lot of people in your situation underestimate how much the environment piece can be worked with. There's specific work we can do around building new routines tied to your shifts, connecting with others in recovery who actually get the industry. You don't have to redesign your whole life. You redesign the pieces that weren't working.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That makes sense. I think I've been seeing it as all or nothing — like either I'm a bartender who drinks or I'm some completely different person. But maybe it's more like... adjusting. Making it fit differently. That actually helps.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've done a lot of work just in this one session, and I want to name that. You came in clear-eyed after a really hard detox. You let yourself see a pattern you'd been hiding from. You sat with real grief about what you've lost. You got angry, which tells me you care about your life and your work. And you ended somewhere important — a vision of being present, and a six out of ten that you can get there. That is where we build from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I feel... I actually feel okay. More than okay, honestly. It's a lot but it feels like I'm actually dealing with it now instead of just drowning it out. That's new for me. I'll take it.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. I'll be honest — a lot of people don't come back for a second session, so the fact that you're here says something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's been going on since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Same stuff. Work's fine, I guess. Come home, have a few drinks, watch TV, go to bed. Nothing earth-shattering. I don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not much has changed, and part of you is wondering what the point of being here even is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... look, my buddy went through something similar a few years back and he said this helped him. So I figured I'd give it another shot. But I'm not — I don't have like, a drinking problem. I just drink. A lot of guys my age drink. It helps me sleep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would make coming here feel worth your time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Stop feeling like garbage every morning, I guess. I wake up and it's like... ugh. But that's just getting older, right? That's not the drinking. I'm forty-eight, everything hurts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The mornings are rough. And at the same time, you're not ready to pin that on the drinking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not the drinking. It's — she left. She took the kids and she left and I'm supposed to just... what? Sit in that house and be fine? Because I'm not fine. And everyone acts like I should be over it by now. Four months. Like that's supposed to be enough time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four months is nothing. Tell me about the house — what's it like coming home to it now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... quiet. That's the thing. It's so damn quiet. The kids used to — my daughter used to have the TV blasting and my son would be on his Xbox and Lisa would be yelling at both of them to turn it down and I used to hate all that noise and now I'd... anyway. It's fine. I handle it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That quiet is brutal. And a drink or two takes the edge off it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well, what else am I supposed to do? She made her choice. I'm not gonna sit there and cry about it. That's not — I don't do that. I just deal with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm curious — what do you think would happen if you did?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What, cry? I... I don't know. I haven't. Not once. Four months and I haven't... [pause] I don't know why I just said that like it was something to be proud of.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four months of carrying all of that. That's a tremendous amount of weight.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I keep thinking about my son. He's fourteen. And when I pick him up on weekends he looks at me like... I don't know. Like he's not sure about me. Like he's watching me. And I don't know if I'm imagining it or if that's real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that look feel like, when you catch it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like I'm... like I'm losing him too. And I can't — I can't lose him too. That's the part I can't think about for too long or I'll lose my mind.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's the divorce, the quiet house, the rough mornings — and sitting underneath all of it is this fear that you're losing your son. That if something doesn't shift, that relationship slips away too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [long pause] Yeah. That's... yeah. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture where the drinking takes you — five years from now — what do you see?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dad. I see my dad. He drank. We weren't — we were never close, me and him. He was just kind of... absent. Even when he was in the room, you know? I swore I was never gonna be that guy. And now I'm sitting in the same chair he used to sit in, having the same number of drinks he used to have. That's... that's a hard thing to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see yourself becoming him. And that terrifies you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want my kid to feel the way I felt. Like his dad just... checked out. I didn't check out. I just — I don't know how to do any of this without her. Twenty years. We were together twenty years. I don't even know who I am without that. [voice cracks] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize for that. Not here. I want to ask you something — and I want you to answer it honestly, not the way you think you're supposed to. What do you actually want for yourself going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be the dad he needs. I want to wake up and not feel like I got hit by a bus. I want to... I don't know, feel like myself again. Some version of myself. And I think — I think I need to do something about the drinking. Like, actually do something. Not just say it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back today when you had every reason not to. You sat with some things that are genuinely painful — your son, your dad, twenty years of your life. And just now you said something that I think took real courage: I need to actually do something. That's not nothing. That's where we can start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [pause] Yeah. I think... I think I'm ready to actually talk about it. For real this time. Not just go through the motions.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in. Walk-ins can feel a little uncertain — you're not always sure what you're walking into. So what brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, honestly? My friends basically made me. Like, they did this whole... thing last week, called it an intervention, and now everyone's on my case to 'talk to someone.' I don't really think I need to be here, I just — yeah. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your friends pushed you to come, and there's a part of you that's genuinely not sure this is even necessary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I drink on weekends. Everyone does. It's college, it's senior year — I don't understand why they're making it into this massive thing. Like I'm some kind of... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think they actually saw that worried them enough to sit you down like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, man. There was this one party a few weeks ago and I fell — on some stairs — and they completely lost it. Called an ambulance. I hit my head a little bit but I was fine. They just... blew it out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still came in, though. Even feeling like you didn't need to. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I mean. I came because otherwise they wouldn't leave me alone. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk me through what a typical weekend looks like for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thursday night usually there's a pregame or something. Friday, Saturday — bars, parties, whatever's going on. It's just... that's what everyone does. I have friends, I go out, I drink. That's college.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned falling on the stairs and hitting your head. What actually happened that night — like, how much had you had?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I — look, I had a lot to drink, okay? I don't even totally remember the stairs part, my friend told me after. I woke up and I was fine, I had a headache, but like — the ambulance thing was so unnecessary. That's what I mean, they just freaked out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't totally remember the stairs. And you're saying it wasn't a big deal — but your friends called an ambulance, staged an intervention, and here you are in a counselor's office. I'm just noticing the gap between those two things.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah, okay, they were scared, I get it. But they overreacted. I have a hard head, I've always been like that. *laughs a little* I'm not — I'm not some drunk who blacks out every weekend. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check that I've got this right. You're out Thursday, Friday, Saturday most weeks. A few weeks ago you had so much that you don't remember falling, hit your head hard enough that your friends called an ambulance. And you're here now — not because you think anything's wrong, but because the people closest to you were scared enough to stage an intervention. That's the picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds way worse than it is. I'm not — I'm a normal college student. I'm not like some guy with a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I be straight with you for a second? Not to pile on — I just think you deserve a real answer instead of me dancing around it. What you're describing, Thursday through Saturday, drinking to the point of not remembering things — that meets the clinical definition of binge drinking. That's not a character attack. It's just what the pattern looks like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay but 'binge drinking' sounds like some after-school special. I'm not drinking in the morning, I'm not missing class, I'm not — like, there are people way worse than me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if drinking were actually becoming a problem for you — what would that look like? In your own definition.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess like... if I was failing out. Or if I couldn't hold it together. Or drinking alone all the time. I'm not doing any of that. I still go to class, I have people who care about me... *pauses* ...I mean my grades haven't been great but that's just — senior year is hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The grades thing — you kind of slid that in at the end, quietly. Like you almost didn't want to say it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Last semester was rough. I got a D in one of my major classes, had to retake a module. But I mean — a lot of people struggle senior year. That's not, like, evidence of anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you line it all up — the grades, the fall, not remembering parts of the night, your friends scared enough to do an intervention — what do you actually make of all that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... *long pause* ...I don't know. I've never put it all together like that before. It's a lot when you — yeah. I don't know. It feels like a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here ready to argue, which makes sense given how you got here. But right now you're actually sitting with it. Not just deflecting. That's harder than it sounds.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not — I'm still not saying I have a problem. I just... I don't know. Maybe it's worth thinking about. I'm not committing to anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here defensive and ready to leave. And somewhere in this conversation something shifted — you started talking about your grades, about not remembering that night, about what your friends saw. You're not shutting the door all the way anymore. I just want to name that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I just — I don't want to be the guy who has a problem and doesn't even see it. That'd be embarrassing. I've got job applications in, I have plans, I don't want this to like... define me or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not what your friends want, not what I think — what do you actually want for yourself going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to feel like it's a choice. Like I'm choosing to go out, not just... doing it because it's Saturday. I don't know if I feel that way right now. Maybe that's the thing I need to figure out.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, look who showed up. Glad you're back — honestly, I wasn't sure if I'd scared you off last week with all my questions. How've you been since we talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I thought about not coming, like genuinely almost texted to cancel this morning. But, I don't know, stuff happened this week and I guess I needed somewhere to, um... I don't know. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You almost bailed but something made you come anyway. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. My dad found out. About the coach thing, the ultimatum, all of it. He called me Sunday night and... yeah, that wasn't fun. He didn't yell or anything, which was almost worse? He just got really quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet is sometimes louder than yelling. What was going through your head during that call?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I wanted to make excuses. Like my first instinct was to be like, 'Coach is overreacting, it's just how college is, everyone parties.' But I couldn't even get the words out. My dad drove six hours to every single home game this year. Six hours. And I just... I don't know, I kind of froze.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The excuses were right there, ready to go — and then they just... didn't come. Like some part of you knew they wouldn't hold up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. Because he knows, right? He's not an idiot. And I think I've been — okay this is gonna sound bad — I think I've been kind of lying to myself about how bad it's gotten. Like not lying lying, but... not looking at it straight.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'how bad it's gotten' — what does that actually look like for you? What are you seeing when you do look at it straight?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My 40 time is up almost half a second from last spring. Half a second. That's... in my position that's the difference between a shot at the draft and not. And I've missed two film sessions. My grades are — I'm on academic watch. I didn't even tell you that last time. I'm on academic watch and if I lose my scholarship I don't know how my family... we're not — my parents aren't, like, rich. This isn't just about football.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to be carrying around, man. The draft, the scholarship, your family's finances — all of that's real and it's all connected. And the fact that you're naming it out loud instead of burying it? That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's terrifying. Like I said it to you just now and my heart's going. I don't think I've actually let myself think about it all at once before. I just kind of... kept it in compartments.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does football actually mean to you? Not the scholarship, not the draft — I mean what is it, at its core, for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... God. Um. I've been playing since I was seven. My dad coached my pee-wee team. Some of my best memories are just, like, summer practices, being exhausted, the team staying after. It's the only thing I've ever been... really good at. Like genuinely good at. School's always been hard for me, I'm not naturally smart like some guys. But on the field I just — I know who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Football's not just a sport for you — it's where you know who you are. And it sounds like it's also this thread that runs through you and your dad.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He never played past high school. Blew his knee out senior year. I think... I think I'm doing it for both of us in some way. And I've been pissing it away at parties and I don't even — I don't even like drinking that much. Isn't that messed up? I'm not even doing it because I love it. I'm doing it because it's just what happens, everyone goes, and I go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said something that I want to sit with for a second — 'I don't even like it that much.' When you picture throwing all of this away for something you're not even that into... what comes up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I feel sick. Genuinely like, I feel sick right now thinking about it. Because it's not — I keep telling myself it's social, it's team bonding, the guys will think I'm weird if I don't go. But my actual teammates, my tight five? They've been covering for me at practice. They're not saying anything. They're just... covering. And that's worse somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, tell me if I get anything wrong. You came back today even though part of you wanted to bail — and something happened this week that made that feel necessary. Your dad found out, and instead of the excuses coming, they just stopped. When you actually look at it straight — the 40 time, the missed sessions, academic watch — it scares you. And underneath all of that is this thing football means to you, something about knowing who you are, and this connection to your dad. And then you said something that really stood out: you're not even sure you like drinking. You're going because it's the path of least resistance. That's a lot to take in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's pretty much all of it. When you say it like that it sounds really obvious. Why didn't I — I've been going to these things for like two years without asking myself any of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sometimes we need someone to hold the mirror. So here's something I'm curious about — forget what your coach wants, forget what your dad wants. What kind of guy do you want to be? Like five years from now, whoever you are after football, what do you want to be able to say about how you handled this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone my teammates could count on. That's the thing that's been eating at me more than the coach stuff, honestly. I'm a captain. I got voted captain. And captains don't... they don't make their guys cover for them at practice. That's not what that's supposed to look like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being someone your team can count on — that matters more to you right now than anything we've talked about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah it really does. I mean the scholarship, the draft stuff, that's all real. But my guys... I look at them in the huddle and I know they're wondering if I'm gonna show up. I can feel it. And I put that there. I did that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got a real clear picture of what you don't want. I'm wondering — what would it actually look like to start being that guy again? What's one thing that feels real, not perfect, just real?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I could just... stop going to Thursday nights. That's the main one, that's when things get out of hand. I always tell myself I'll just go for an hour and then it's four in the morning. If I just don't go to Thursdays — I can still hang with the guys, I can still be social, but Thursday nights I'm done. I think I could actually do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just came up with that yourself, and it's specific and it's yours. That matters. You're not talking about some extreme overhaul — you know your own pattern well enough to identify the thing that needs to change.

utterances.speaker: client
