utterances.text: I mean, honestly? I feel lighter right now than I have in months. Like I came in here this morning dreading this and now I'm kind of — I don't want to jinx it, but I actually feel like I can do something about it. Which is new.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to hold onto that feeling with you, not let it evaporate when you leave. So let me just reflect back where we've landed today: you came in carrying a lot — your dad, the coach ultimatum, the stuff you've been avoiding looking at. And you didn't run from any of it today. You've got a reason that's bigger than the drinking itself — being the kind of captain you want to be. And you've got a concrete first step in Thursday nights. Before you head out — what would help you actually remember all this when Thursday rolls around and someone texts you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly I think I might just tell Marcus — he's my co-captain. Tell him what I'm doing. Because if he knows, then it's real. I can't fake it with Marcus, he'll call me out. And I kind of want that. I think I actually want someone to hold me to it this time.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, please — make yourself comfortable. I'm glad you found us today. I know walk-in visits can feel a little... uncertain. What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, my — the woman over at the senior center, she kept after me about coming. I didn't really want to bother anyone, but she practically walked me here herself. I'm not even sure I belong here, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She cared enough to make sure you got here. And you came. That says something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I suppose. I just... I don't really know what I'm supposed to say. I'm 72 years old. I've been handling things on my own my whole life. I don't know what good talking is going to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seventy-two years of handling things on your own. That's a long time to carry everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. And I want you to know right away — I am not some kind of... I'm not a drunk. I have pain. Real pain, in my hips, my lower back. The pills they give me, they only go so far. And a person has to sleep somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The pain is real. Tell me more about what that's like for you, day to day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Some mornings I can barely get out of bed. I used to garden, you know. I had the most beautiful garden. Now I just... I look out the window at it. Last Tuesday I was up at three in the morning because there is just no position, no comfortable position at all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Up at three in the morning, alone with that pain...

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And what am I supposed to do? My doctor, he just refills the prescription and sends me home. He doesn't really — he doesn't listen. So yes. A glass of wine at night, sometimes two, it takes the edge off. It helps me sleep. I don't see why that's so terrible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And your family — what do they see when they look at you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They worry too much. My daughter found some bottles and she got very upset. She called my son and then they both called me on the same day, and it turned into this whole... thing. I felt like I was being ganged up on. I'm their mother, for goodness sake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It felt like an ambush. When you were just trying to get through your days.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And the last thing I want is to be a burden to them. They have their own lives, their own children to worry about. I am not going to call my daughter at three in the morning because my hip hurts. I'm just not going to do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You are protecting them. Even in the middle of your own pain — your first thought is them. That is... that is a very deep kind of love.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I never thought of it quite that way. I just thought I was being sensible. Not making a fuss. But... yes. I suppose that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think it would mean to your daughter — if she really knew how much pain you were in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She'd be devastated. She'd find a way to blame herself, she always does. But... honestly? I think she already knows. She's not a foolish girl. And maybe that's worse somehow. That she knows and she doesn't know what to do either. We're both just... stuck.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Carrying it alone. Together.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hm. Yeah. I hadn't... yeah. We don't talk about hard things in our family. Never have. My mother was exactly the same way. You just — you endure. You don't make a fuss.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just... reflect back what I'm hearing, if that's alright. You've been living with serious, real pain for a long time. The medication isn't enough, and the alcohol gives you some relief, some sleep. You love your family more than anything and you have been doing everything you can not to frighten them. And somewhere in the middle of all of that — I wonder if anyone has actually stopped to ask how you are really doing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... No. No, they don't ask that. They ask about my pills, my appointments, whether I've eaten. They don't ask... they don't really ask about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... I'm scared, if I'm being honest with you. I know mixing things isn't smart, I'm not a foolish woman. But I don't know another way to get through the night. And I'm scared that if I say that out loud to my children, they'll just panic and start making decisions for me. And I'll end up... I don't know. Somewhere I don't want to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to say. And I hear you clearly — you want a say in what happens next. You don't want to be rescued. You want to be heard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. That's — yes, exactly. I've been thinking, since she found those bottles... maybe there is something else. Maybe there is a way to get through the night that doesn't scare everybody. Including me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to share something with you, if that's alright — not to frighten you, but because you deserve to know the full picture. Mixing alcohol with certain pain medications can genuinely be dangerous. It can affect breathing, the heart. What you've been doing isn't weakness — your body has been doing whatever it could to cope with real suffering. And there are actually some good options. Pain specialists who really listen, sleep support, some newer approaches that have helped people in very similar situations. You wouldn't have to figure any of it out alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't realize it was that serious. I mean — I suspected, I'm not naive. But hearing it said plainly like that... okay. Okay. What would that even look like, getting some help with this?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I love that you're asking that. What would feel like a manageable first step to you — something small, something that feels like it's yours?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... maybe finding a different doctor. One who actually listens to me. And maybe letting my daughter come with me. She'd want to, I know she would. I've just been... too proud, I suppose. Too used to doing things alone. But it might be time to let someone in.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I want to start there, because that took something. How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I... I wasn't sure I would, honestly. But here I am. I guess that counts for something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What made you decide to come back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean — I do know. I was sitting there Sunday night and I just thought, this isn't who I am. Or... it's not who I was. And I want to be that person again. I just don't know if I can.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That person you were for three years. You haven't forgotten him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't. And that's — that's almost the hardest part, you know? Because I remember exactly what it felt like. Waking up clear. Having a routine. Feeling like I was actually showing up for my life. And then I just... blew it all up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk me through what happened. The job loss, and then — what did those first few days actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They called me in on a Friday. Seventeen years with that company, and it was like a twenty-minute meeting. I drove home and I just sat in my car in the parking lot for... I don't even know how long. I didn't know what to do with myself. That night, I bought a bottle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The rug got completely pulled out from under you. And that bottle — what was it doing for you in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... shut the noise off. That's the only way I can describe it. The shame, the panic, the — what am I gonna tell people, what does this mean. It all just went quiet for a little while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And then it came back louder.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. God, yeah. The next morning was... I hadn't felt like that in three years. The shaky hands, the sick stomach. And I thought, what have I done. Three years. And then I drank again because I couldn't face it. That's when I knew I was in real trouble.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You recognized it fast. A lot of people don't catch it that quickly — that's not a small thing. But I'm also hearing a lot of shame underneath all of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah. I'm ashamed. I worked really hard for those three years. I had a sponsor. I did the steps. I went to meetings every week for the first year and a half. And I just... threw it away. Over a job. It's pathetic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is that what you actually believe — that you're pathetic?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Some days. I'm fifty years old. I feel like I should have more control than this. Like I should know better by now. And whenever I think about calling my sponsor, going back to a meeting... I just can't face those people. I can't walk back in there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're angry at yourself. And scared of what people will think.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm furious at myself. Three years. I had a life. I was sleeping right, I was showing up, I felt like an actual person. And now I'm back to hiding bottles and making excuses and I just... I am so tired of starting over. I'm so tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That exhaustion is real. Starting over is hard. And you've done it before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I know. I know I have. But it felt different when I was younger, I had more — more fight in me, I guess. Now I look in the mirror and I think, is this just who I am? Is this just my life?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That question — 'is this just who I am' — what's underneath that? What are you really telling yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That maybe I don't deserve it. The sobriety. The good life. My kids barely call anymore. My ex-wife moved on years ago. The job was the last thing I had that made me feel like I was worth something. And I lost that too.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's a lot in here. You lost something that meant everything — not just the income, but your sense of worth, your identity. And in that pain, you reached for the one thing that's ever made it go quiet. And now you're carrying shame about that on top of the grief. And yet — underneath all of it — there is still a man who remembers what it felt like to be well. Who drove himself back here today because some part of him is not ready to give up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. Yeah, that's... the grief part. I hadn't thought of it like that. But yeah. I think I've been grieving a lot of things for a long time, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about something that mattered to you during those three years. Something real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I coached my nephew's little league team one summer. Showed up every single practice, in a good mood, clear-headed. And I remember driving home after one of the games and just thinking — this is it. This is what a life feels like. I hadn't felt that in... a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That man is still in there. The one who showed up for his nephew, who did the steps, who built three years from nothing. You've been using that memory to beat yourself up — 'you had it and you threw it away.' But that memory also means you know exactly what you're capable of. That's not a wound. That's a map.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I never thought about it that way. I've just been using it to punish myself. But you're saying — it means I've done it. It means I know the way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built it before. You know the path, and you know what's on it — AA, your sponsor, all of it. So let me ask you this: what's one thing, just one small thing this week, that would feel true to the person you want to be again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I want to call my sponsor. I've been avoiding it because I'm scared of what he'll say, or — I don't know, that he'll be disappointed. But he's relapsed before too. He told me that. I think if I just called him and said, hey, I messed up... I think he'd understand. Yeah. That's the one thing. I can do that.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I know the waiting room out there is not exactly a five-star experience — appreciate you hanging around. So Dr. Patel mentioned you might be coming by. No agenda today, seriously, just want to get a sense of what's been going on for you. What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... I don't really know where to start, honestly. Things with my PhD have been, um... rough. Like, really rough. And I've been drinking more than I probably should to deal with it. I guess that's the thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking has become kind of a way to get through it — especially when the thesis stuff feels like too much.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: More like get through the night, yeah. I work all day, or I try to, and then by like 8 or 9 PM I just... I don't know. I pour a drink and somehow that's the only time my brain actually shuts up a little. Which sounds bad when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What is your brain usually saying when it won't shut up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I'm not supposed to be there. That everyone in my cohort is just... killing it, and I'm falling behind. My advisor actually said — and I'm basically quoting — 'this draft lacks the rigor I expect from you.' Like, okay. Cool. Super helpful feedback, thanks. So there's that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot to carry. The pressure of the program, your advisor's words landing a certain way, feeling like you're behind everyone else — and you're still showing up and putting in the hours. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. It doesn't feel like much when you're staring at a blank page for three hours. And then you drink and for a little while it's like — okay, I can breathe. But then the next morning is just worse, so... I don't know. It's not really working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does 'worse' look like the next morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like — okay, so I'm not, I want to be clear, I'm not drinking in the morning or anything like that. But if I have four, five drinks, which has been happening more lately, then I'm foggy. I have this low-grade anxiety all day. And the thing is... the exact thing I'm scared of — my work not being good enough — I'm literally causing that by doing this. I know that. Like I genuinely know that and I still do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see the whole cycle clearly — and that's actually the hardest part. Knowing something isn't helping you but it still feels like the only off switch you've got.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And it's not like — I mean, I'm not an alcoholic or whatever. I barely drank in undergrad. Like this is genuinely new for me. I just... I don't know how it got here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when you got into the PhD program. What changed?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything? The stakes feel completely different. In undergrad if I bombed a paper it's like, okay, whatever, move on. But this is five years. This is my career. And — I don't know if this is too much to say — I grew up not having a lot, and getting into this program felt like I'd finally made it, you know? Like finally. And now every single day I'm terrified I'm going to blow it. That it's going to turn out I wasn't actually good enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm hearing you right. You came into this program with a lot on the line — not just a degree but something that means something deep about where you've come from and who you're becoming. The pressure has been enormous, and the drinking started as a way to quiet all of that. But you're watching it work against you — the foggy mornings, the anxiety, the work slipping — and you're stuck watching yourself do the very thing that makes what you're scared of more likely to happen.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I hadn't put it together quite like that but that's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you actually imagine finishing — like defending your dissertation, being done — what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... I think about it a lot, actually. I'd be the first person in my family with a doctorate. My mom would just — she would lose it, in a good way. And I'd actually get to contribute something real, you know? Like the whole reason I picked this topic is because I think it matters and nobody's really looked at it this way before. I have ideas. Like, actual ideas. It's just... right now I can't access any of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the work itself still means something to you. This isn't just about surviving the program — there's something you actually want to say, something you want to contribute.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I do. And that's the thing that really gets me, right? Because I feel like I'm slowly taking apart the only thing that would actually get me there. Like I'm sabotaging the version of myself that could do this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being able to see that clearly — even from inside it — that's not easy. A lot of people can't get there for a long time, if ever.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if that makes me feel better or worse. Like... okay maybe a little better? I just — I don't want to be the guy who had the shot and didn't take it. Like that would genuinely break me. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you if you got the drinking back under control — not perfectly, not overnight, just back to where it's not running things?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd be less scared all the time. Like, honestly, some of what I'm calling imposter syndrome might just be... being hungover and foggy every day. If I actually showed up clear, maybe my work would improve and maybe my advisor would back off, and maybe it wouldn't feel so... I don't know. Maybe it wouldn't feel so hopeless.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So getting some of that clarity back might actually start to loosen the whole thing — not just the drinking but the self-doubt, the work, the relationship with your advisor.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And I keep saying 'I don't know how to do this anymore' but... I do. I know how to work hard. I've been doing it my whole life. I just — somewhere in the last year I kind of lost the thread. But I think it's still there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you know how to do this. If you were going to take one small step — not overhaul everything, just one concrete thing this week — what feels actually doable?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I could try to not drink on weeknights. That's where most of it is happening anyway. It's like, Tuesday night when I'm panicking about a meeting, that's the danger zone. Weekends are usually fine. So yeah — weeknights. I think I could try that and see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real, specific plan — and it's yours, you built it. So let me pull together what I've heard today. You came in carrying a lot — the pressure, the feedback, the fear that maybe you don't belong there. And underneath all of it is someone who knows exactly why he's doing this: for himself, for his mom, because he actually has something to say. The drinking made sense as a way to cope when everything got loud. But you've been watching it chip away at the very thing you're fighting for, and you're not okay with that. So this week — no drinking on weeknights, see how it lands. And I want to say this: the fact that you walked in here today, that you were honest about all of it? That's the thread you said was still there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I needed to hear all of that out loud. I've been... kind of avoiding this conversation for a while. Thanks for not making it weird.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. Grab a seat wherever — yeah, that one's fine, the other one has a broken armrest that'll make you feel like you're slowly sliding out of the conversation. Not ideal.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So — and there's no wrong answer here — what made you decide to come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't really decide. My parents basically said I had to, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this is more about keeping the peace at home than anything you actually wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pretty much, yeah. I don't even — like, I don't have a problem. They just freaked out over nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know what, showing up when you really don't want to? That actually takes something. Most people just... don't. So I appreciate that you're here, even if it feels like a waste of time right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I didn't really have a choice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what actually happened — from your side of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My mom went through my room — which, by the way, is a complete invasion of privacy — and she found some bottles under my bed. A few beers, some vodka. And they just completely lost it. Called my dad at work, the whole thing. It was so dramatic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: They went full DEFCON-1 and you felt like the response just didn't match what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like yeah okay, I had some drinks, whatever. Every kid does that. It's not... I'm not some alcoholic or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does drinking actually do for you? Like what's the appeal — what do you get out of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's... it just, like, turns everything down a little. You know? School is stressful, home is stressful, and when I drink it's just... quieter. In my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like noise-cancelling headphones, but for your brain.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Kind of. I never thought about it like that but — yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot of noise to be dealing with. What's making things loud at home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My parents have been... I don't know. Fighting a lot. Not screaming or whatever, but just this constant tension. And I kind of feel like I have to stay out of their way. And my grades haven't been great either. I just — sometimes I don't want to think about any of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you've been carrying a lot — trying to stay invisible at home, school pressure on top of that — and drinking became a way to get some relief from all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I didn't think it was a big deal. But when my mom was crying — like actually crying at the kitchen table — that was kind of hard to watch. She was really scared.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That landed differently than you expected it to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I was so angry when it all went down but then she was just... at the table, crying, and I felt like an idiot. Like, she wasn't being dramatic. She was just scared. And I did that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just make sure I'm tracking all of this. You've been dealing with a lot — tension at home, school not going great, and drinking became the way to get some quiet from all that noise. You walked in here pretty sure this was going to be pointless. But somewhere underneath the 'I don't have a problem' thing... there's a kid who didn't like seeing his mom cry. And now you're actually sitting here thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I hate that that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — fair. So here's what I'm actually curious about: if things could be different — not what your parents want, not what I want — what would you want for yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I want things to feel less like everything's about to fall apart all the time. And like — I want to not have to hide stuff. That's actually exhausting, keeping track of where everything is, making sure they don't find anything. I didn't even realize how much until right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The hiding was almost as heavy as whatever you were hiding from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it really was. I don't know if I want to stop drinking completely but I — I don't want it to be like this. The sneaking around thing. I don't want to be that person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's actually a significant thing to figure out in forty-five minutes — you came in here not wanting to be here, and you're leaving with something real. So just one thing: what's one small step this week? Not an overhaul, not a big promise. Just one thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I could actually talk to my mom. Not like a whole big thing, just — let her know I heard her, I guess. And maybe come back here? Like, if that's okay.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, make yourself comfortable. I'm Dr. Reyes. There's water on the table if you want some. So — before we get into anything formal, what's it like being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Fine, I guess. I've been to clinics before, for physical things. This is... different. My employer said I had to come, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because someone else said you had to be. That's worth naming. And I'm curious — setting aside what your employer wants — what's your own read on why you're sitting in this chair?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... there was an incident at work. I don't want to lose my job. That's it, honestly. I don't think I need, like, counseling or whatever this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Keeping your job matters to you. That makes a lot of sense. Can you tell me a bit about what happened — the incident, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came in... not great, one morning. Someone smelled something and reported it. It wasn't — I mean, I wasn't drunk. I'd had a couple drinks the night before and I guess I still smelled like it. It was embarrassing. Really embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a hard morning. Embarrassing in front of colleagues, then having to deal with HR on top of it. You mentioned a couple drinks the night before — what does a typical evening look like for you these days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home, I... make dinner sometimes, or order something. I have a glass of wine. Maybe two. Three on bad days. It's — I know how that sounds. But I'm not like, an alcoholic. I function. I go to work every day, I pay my bills.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding a lot together. Job, bills, daily life — in a country that's not where you grew up, if I'm reading your file right. That's genuinely not easy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I moved here two years ago. I don't... I don't have family here. No real friends yet. It's just me and my apartment, basically.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Just you and your apartment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean, it's quieter here than where I'm from. Back home there was always someone around — my mom, my cousins, neighbors just dropping by. Here people just... don't do that. Everyone is very busy with their own lives.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You went from a world that was full of people — just constantly around — to somewhere where the evenings are really, really quiet. What does that feel like, when you walk in after work and it's just... silent?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... it's hard to explain. Like, I chose this. I wanted to come here, I worked for it. So I feel stupid complaining. But some nights it's just — the silence is really loud, you know? That's a weird thing to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, that's not weird at all. The silence is loud. That actually says it really well. And I wonder if that's when the wine comes in — when the silence gets too loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yes. I don't even really like the taste that much anymore. It just — it takes the edge off. Fills the room a little, somehow. I know that sounds pathetic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound pathetic. It sounds like you found something that worked, at least for a while. You were hurting and you found a way to get through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. But now it's... now it's costing me. My job is at risk. I'm tired all the time. I don't — I'm not happy. I thought coming here would make me happy, eventually. I kept waiting for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came here with real hope. And two years in, the happiness hasn't shown up the way you imagined. That's a painful gap to sit with. What does happy look like to you — if you picture it, what's actually in that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: People. Honestly, just... people. Someone to eat dinner with. Someone who knows my name beyond just coworkers. Back home I had that everywhere. Here I have to — I don't know — build it from nothing. And I don't know how to do that as an adult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Building connection from zero, as a grown adult in a new place — that is genuinely one of the harder things a person can do. And what I'm hearing underneath all of this is that the drinking was never really about alcohol. It was about loneliness.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think that's right. I never said it that way but... that's it. That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if we were to work on something together — not just get through this referral, but actually work on something — the real thing to work on might be the isolation, not just the drinking. Does that feel true to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yes. But that feels scarier than just stopping drinking, honestly. Drinking I can try to control. I don't know how to just... make friends. At 29. It feels embarrassing to even say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes courage to say the real thing out loud. A lot of people come in here and we spend months dancing around it. You just went straight to the center of it in one session. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm — thank you. I don't know, I thought I was going to come in here and you'd be like, 'how much do you drink per week' and hand me a pamphlet. This is... this feels different. Like maybe there's actually something to figure out here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There is something to figure out. And I want to reflect back what you've shared today, because I think you should hear it all in one place: you made a brave move coming here, to a whole new country. You've been carrying that transition mostly alone. The drinking became a way to manage the silence and the loneliness — and it worked until it didn't. And what you actually want isn't less alcohol, it's more connection. That's a very human thing to want.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... When you say it like that it doesn't feel like a character flaw. It just feels like a problem I can actually, maybe, solve.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is a problem you can work on. And you don't have to do it alone — that's actually the whole point. If you were willing to come back, what would feel like a small but real first step between now and next week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I saw there's like a community group at the library. For immigrants, actually. I walked past it once and kept walking. Maybe I could just — go. Just go and see. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you coming in today. I know the ER's not exactly... restful. How are you feeling right now, just sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. I mean — I've been in worse places. This is just... I don't know why they sent me here, honestly. I'm not some kind of — I don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't plan on being here. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean — look, I had a rough night. That's it. People have rough nights. Doesn't mean I need to be sitting in... whatever this is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the rough night. What was going on for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just — I drank too much. Okay? It happens. I was... it was the kids' birthday. Well, their birthdays are a week apart, so we used to do one big thing. And this year I wasn't there. She didn't — I wasn't invited. So. I drank too much and I ended up in the ER, that's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Missing that... that sounds really painful.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's fine. I mean — it's not fine, but — I'm dealing with it. I've got a lot going on. The divorce was finalized two months ago, I've been trying to get back on my feet, got a new apartment. It's a lot. But I'm handling it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot on your plate — the apartment, the divorce, missing the kids' birthday. And on top of all that, you're here, talking to a stranger.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I didn't exactly have a choice. The ER doc basically said come here or... some other option I didn't like. So here I am. But I want to be clear — I'm not an alcoholic. I know what those guys look like, okay? I've been around. I served. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that look like to you — those guys you've seen?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Guys who can't hold it together. Guys who lost everything and they're still — they just kept going. I still have my job. I still show up. I call my kids every Sunday. I'm not... I'm not that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've held onto things that matter — your job, staying connected to your kids every week. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. It's getting harder. I'll say that. The Sunday calls... they're hard. My daughter, she's twelve, she doesn't say much anymore. I don't know if she's mad at me or if that's just — I don't know. And my son, he's nine, he still asks when I'm coming home and I just — I don't know what to tell him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: He asks when you're coming home... and you don't have an answer for him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't have a goddamn answer. No. And then I hang up and I — yeah. I drink. Because what am I supposed to do with that? Just sit there? Just sit there and feel it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happens when you imagine just... sitting with it? Without the drink?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't — I tried, actually. Couple nights ago I tried to just go to sleep. Couldn't. Everything just... it gets loud. You know what I mean? It gets real loud in here and I can't — I need it to quiet down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gets loud. And the drinking quiets it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: For a while. Yeah. And then... then I wake up and it's worse. It's always worse in the morning. I know that. I know that and I do it anyway, and that's the part that — I don't know what that says about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think it says about you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I'm a guy who's really, really tired. I'm exhausted. I had a whole life. We were together twenty-two years. And now I've got this apartment that smells like new paint, and I eat cereal for dinner, and my kids are fifteen minutes away and it might as well be — ... I don't know. I'm just tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. That's not just a relationship ending. That's a whole world.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. And I keep — I keep being angry because it's easier to be angry than... than this. This right here. This is — ... sorry. I didn't think I was gonna do this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. Not here. You don't have to apologize for that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just — I miss my family. That's the thing I can't say out loud. Because everybody wants to talk about the drinking or the divorce or whatever, but underneath all of it, that's — that's what it is. I just miss them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that grief mostly alone, and it sounds like the drinking has been the only thing that's given you any relief from it — even just for a few hours. I'm also hearing something else: a dad who calls every Sunday, who still shows up, who came in today even when he didn't want to. And I'm wondering — when you imagine things looking different a year from now, what would you want that to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want my kids to not be worried about me. I want to be the dad they call when something good happens, not just — not because they have to check in. And I think right now... I don't think I'm that guy. Not yet. But maybe — I don't know, maybe I could be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That matters. The fact that you can see that — the dad you want to be — that's real. And walking in here today, that wasn't nothing. That was actually something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I don't know what I'm doing. I really don't. But maybe... maybe I can figure something out. I'm not saying I've got it all figured out. But... yeah. Maybe.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know that's not always easy to do. There's no agenda here, no checklist we have to get through — just whatever feels right to talk about. So, what brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My friend basically made me. She pulled this whole... intervention thing, which felt really dramatic. I mean I appreciate that she cares, I guess, but I don't really think I have a problem. Like, I drink some wine at night, that's it. I'm a grown adult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your friend pushed pretty hard, and part of you is still not sure this is even the right place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. Like, I have two kids, I work full time, I manage the whole house by myself — my ex is basically useless — and I am holding it together. You know? So I'm not sure what the big emergency is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That really is a lot to carry. What does the end of a typical day actually look like for you — after the kids are down and everything's done?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home, make dinner, help with homework — my youngest has been struggling in math so that's, like, a whole thing — deal with whatever fight they're having, get them to bed. And then I sit down and I pour a glass of wine. Is that a crime? I've earned it. It's the only five minutes in the day that are actually mine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That glass of wine is yours. The one thing in the whole day that isn't about someone else needing something from you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And now everyone's making me feel like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I'm some kind of addict or something. I'm not sitting in a gutter somewhere. I function. I show up. That counts for something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Absolutely it counts. Can I ask — when you say a glass of wine, roughly how much are we talking on a given night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's usually a bottle. Over the whole evening, not like all at once. And it's wine, not like I'm doing shots or whatever. But... yeah. A bottle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to say that out loud — especially the first time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never actually said it like that to anyone. It sounds... it sounds worse out loud, doesn't it. When you just say it like a number.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hearing it out loud lands differently than just living with it quietly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I know it's a lot. I'm not oblivious. I just — I genuinely don't know what else to do. When the kids go to bed it's like I just... I crash. And that's the thing that gets me through.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would getting through the night even look like without it, do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have no idea. That's kind of the thing. I've been doing this every night for... god, like two years maybe? More? And I honestly don't know if I can relax without it anymore. Like, I don't remember how. That's kind of scary when I actually think about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not even knowing how to wind down without it — and that uncertainty scares you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. And I've been noticing things. I wake up and I'm just... tired in this different way. Not like normal tired. And headaches. I get these headaches in the morning that I didn't used to get. I kind of know what that means. I just haven't wanted to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those things your body is doing — the tiredness, the headaches — what do you make of them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think it's telling me something. Which is... I've been kind of ignoring that thought for a while now. It's easier to just not go there. But yeah. I think my body's not okay with this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check I'm tracking everything you've shared. You came in today not really convinced you needed to be here — and I respect that you came anyway. You're carrying an enormous amount by yourself, and over time the wine became the one thing that was just for you at the end of the day. And at the same time, you're noticing some physical things that worry you, and you're sitting with this unsettling question of whether you even know how to relax without it anymore. Both of those things seem really true at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's it. God. When you lay it out like that it's a lot. I haven't let myself see all of it at once before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Forget what your friend wants, or what you think I want to hear. What do you actually want for yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to not be so tired. I want to... I want to actually be present with my kids. Because sometimes I'm sitting there at the table with them and I'm just counting down until they go to bed. And I hate that. I hate that I do that. They deserve better than that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being really there for them — that's the whole point for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're why I do all of it. All of it. And I've just been... surviving, I guess. Just getting through. I don't think I've been actually living for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you can see that clearly — and that it genuinely bothers you — that's not a small thing. A lot of people spend years not being able to get to what you just said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came in here ready to argue with you, honestly. I had my whole thing prepared. And now I'm just... I don't know. This is not how I expected this to go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So now that you're here — what feels like it could be a first step, even a really small one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... just this. Being honest about it. Saying it out loud instead of just pretending it's fine. I think that's where I'd have to start. I've been lying to myself for a long time.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi there, it's really good to meet you. I'm glad we could make this work over video. How are you doing right now, just in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, uh... alright I guess. Little strange doing this on a computer. Never done this kind of thing before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something new for you. And I imagine coming here today... wasn't exactly your first choice.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. Judge said I had to. Got a DUI a few months back and... I'm not proud of it. But here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you saying that. It takes something to show up even when it's required. What's a typical day like for you these days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not much. Wake up, have my coffee, watch the morning news. Used to have somewhere to be every day, you know? Retired three years ago and I... I don't know. Days kind of blur together now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The days blur together... like something's been missing since you retired.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Forty years I worked, same place. Then one day you're just... home. And my wife passed two years ago too, so it's really just me rattling around in that house.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot of loss in a short stretch of time — the work, your wife. I imagine the evenings especially can feel very quiet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's exactly it. The evenings. That's when I started... that's when the drinking kind of picked up, I guess. Have one while I watch TV and then somehow it's three or four. I don't always even notice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It kind of crept up on you. What do you make of that — the drinking becoming more of a regular part of the evenings?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's not like I'm some kind of alcoholic. It was just something to do. Something that felt... warm, I suppose. Like having a little company in the room.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It filled something that the quiet couldn't. And your doctor mentioned some concerns at your last visit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, he said my liver numbers were off. Told me I really needed to cut back. I thought about it for a few days and then... honestly I just kept going the same way. Didn't really change anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about hearing it from him stayed with you, even if acting on it felt hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm sixty-five. I know I'm not young anymore. My wife, she didn't make it to sixty-three, and I think about that sometimes. Am I just... am I throwing away whatever years I've got left?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real question you're sitting with. What matters most to you about the years ahead?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My grandkids. Three of them. I want to be around for them, you know? Not just... sitting in a chair getting older. I want to actually do things with them. Be there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The grandkids are really at the heart of this for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And my daughter... she worries. She doesn't say it outright but she calls a lot more than she used to. I know what that means.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I take a moment to share back what I've been hearing from you? You've been carrying a lot — losing your wife, losing the structure that work gave you, the loneliness that settles in during those evenings. Drinking kind of became a way to fill some of that quiet. And at the same time, there's a part of you that hears what your doctor said, that thinks about your grandkids, and wonders whether something needs to shift. Does that feel like it captures it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's pretty much it. I never really laid it all out like that but... that's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you to make a change — not because the judge said so, but because you decided you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I'd feel like myself again. Like the person I was before all this. I used to do woodworking, go fishing. Haven't touched any of that stuff in two years. Just kind of stopped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That person — the one with the woodworking and the fishing trips — he's still in there. You can see him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah, maybe. I've still got all my tools out in the garage. My wife used to tease me — said I had more tools than sense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She sounds like she knew you well. If you were to take one small step this week — just one — what feels like something you could actually do?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... on the evenings when I'd normally just pour a drink, I could go out to the garage instead. Or call my daughter. Just... do something different. I think I could try that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already figured out what pulls you toward the drinking and what might pull you away from it. You came in today because you had to, and somewhere in this conversation you found your own reasons. That's yours — nobody gave that to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't expect to feel... I don't know. A little lighter, I guess. I think I actually want to try this time. Really try.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know this wasn't exactly your idea — your employer set this up. So I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I'd rather do is just hear from you directly. What's your take on being here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't really know. I feel like it's a bit of an overreaction, honestly. One incident and suddenly everyone's got their hair on fire. I've been dealing with a lot lately — my divorce just finalized four months ago — and yeah, maybe I've been drinking more than usual. But I'm not some... I'm not an alcoholic or whatever. I'm handling it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The divorce is still pretty recent. Four months isn't very long.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it's not. And... look, she — my ex — she's the one who ended it. Twenty-two years. We have two kids. And she just... decided she was done. So yeah, I've had a few more drinks in the evening. I think that's pretty understandable.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. And then it's gone. I can understand why you'd need something to take the edge off. Can you tell me a bit more about what a typical evening looks like for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home... to my apartment. I'm renting this — it's a one-bedroom, it's fine. I make something to eat or I don't, and I... have a drink. Watch TV. Maybe have another. I don't know, I'm not keeping a tally. But it's not like I'm blacking out every night or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Coming home to a quiet one-bedroom after twenty-two years in a house with a family — that's a massive shift. That kind of silence can be really loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I... my kids are with her most of the time. I see them every other weekend. My son — he's fifteen — he barely looks at me when I pick him up. I don't know what she's told him. And my daughter, she's twelve, she just cries. Every time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds incredibly painful — watching your kids hurt and feeling like you can't reach them. When you're sitting in that apartment on the nights you don't have them, what goes through your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... a lot of stuff. Anger, mostly. At her. At the whole situation. Sometimes I think about — like, what did I do wrong? Or was it all her? I don't know. And I hate not knowing. I've always been someone who figures things out and I just... I can't figure this out. And the drinking — okay, I know it's gotten more. I'm not stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not stupid. And part of you already knows the drinking has escalated — you just said that out loud. That takes some honesty, even to admit to yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean... I've been waking up at three in the morning lately. Just lying there. And I think, okay, if I have one more drink I'll fall back asleep. Which works, but then I wake up feeling like garbage and I go to work and... that's probably how the incident happened, honestly. I wasn't all there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's starting to bleed into work. What was going through your mind that morning — the morning of the incident?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had had... probably more than I should have the night before. I got into it with my manager over something small and I just — I lost it. Said some things. I've never done that before. Twenty years I've worked there and I've never once been written up. That scared me a little, if I'm honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment scared you. Because it wasn't you — or at least not the version of yourself you recognize.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Yeah. I've always... my dad was a drinker. A bad one. And I swore I'd never be like him. I was the one who had it together. Good job, nice house, coached my kid's soccer team... and now I look around and I'm like — when did this happen? When did I become this person?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The image you had of yourself — who you were supposed to be — it feels like it's slipping. And that matters to you deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. I... I don't want my kids to look back and think their dad fell apart. My son, he's at that age where he's watching everything I do. I can feel it. And I'm drinking away my evenings and getting written up at work and... that's not who I want to be. I just don't know how to stop feeling this way without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What you just said is really important. You know what you don't want — you don't want to be your father, you don't want your kids watching you unravel. So let me ask you this: who do you want to be on the other side of all this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I haven't really thought about it that way. I've just been trying to survive each night. But... I want to be someone my kids can call when something goes wrong. I want to actually show up. My dad never showed up. I always said I would.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being there for your kids — that's still the thing. Even through all of this, that hasn't changed in you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it hasn't. That's... that's probably the one thing I'm sure of right now. Everything else feels like — I don't even know. But that part, yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You've been through something enormous — your marriage ended, you lost the daily life you had with your kids, and the drinking has been a way to get through the nights. But it's starting to cost you: your work, your sleep, your sense of who you are. And underneath all of it, what's driving this isn't really anger — it's grief. And a fear of becoming your father. Of failing your kids the way he failed you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. That's... yeah. I didn't expect anyone to just say it that clearly. I've been telling myself I'm angry at her but I think — I think I'm just really sad. Like, really sad. And scared.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took courage to say. Anger is a lot easier to carry than grief. A lot of people never get to what you just got to. Given everything you've shared today — what feels like a real first step? Not huge. Just real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... not drinking the night before I see my kids? Like, I want to actually be present when I pick them up. Not foggy or half-asleep. That feels like something I could actually try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today thinking this was an overreaction. You've never talked to anyone like this before. And in the past hour, you identified what's really going on and named a concrete step you want to take. That's not nothing — that's actually a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I didn't think I'd... I mean, I was ready to just sit here and wait it out. But this is — it's more useful than I expected. I'm not going to pretend everything's fixed. But I feel like I at least know what I'm dealing with a little better now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Knowing what you're dealing with is the start. If you came back — not because your employer said so, but because you chose to — what would you want to work on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably... figuring out how to get through the nights without reaching for a bottle. And maybe — I don't know — how to actually talk to my son. I've been avoiding it because I don't know what to say. But I think I need to try. Yeah. I think I'd actually come back for that.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, come on in. I'll warn you the couch is more comfortable than it looks — I've had people fall asleep on it, which I honestly take as a win. I'm Reyes. You want some water or anything before we get into it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm good. And Marcus is fine. Look, I'm just here 'cause my therapist — my old therapist — said I needed to come. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. You're here because someone told you to be here. I've had worse reasons for a visit. What's your sense of what they were hoping you'd get out of coming?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They think I drink too much. My wife thinks so too. I mean... I drink, yeah. But I did two tours. You want me to just — what, do yoga? I don't think that's a me thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yoga is officially off the table. Noted. So drinking has been part of how you've managed things since you got back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wouldn't even call it "managing." It's just — that's what guys do. After a patrol, after deployment, you drink. That's not a problem, that's Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes complete sense in context — military culture around drinking is real, that's not something you invented. I'm curious though, what's different now that it's gotten to the point where people are sending you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Nothing's different. People are just... I don't know, more sensitive about it. My wife, she grew up with a dad who drank bad, so she's got her own... thing going on. And she's been reading stuff online and now suddenly I'm an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's scared. Her history makes this hit different for her than it might for someone else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I get that. I do. But it's not the same situation. I'm not — I'm not her dad. I'm functional. I go to work, I handle my stuff. I'm not... it's not like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've probably had to say that more times than you'd like. I want to make sure I understand what we're actually talking about — what does a typical week look like for you? Like when and how much?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Every night, basically. Couple beers after work. Sometimes more on weekends. It's not — I'm not drinking in the morning or anything like that. I'm not hiding bottles in the garage or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So every night, heavier on weekends — and "not hiding bottles" is the bar you're measuring yourself against.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay that sounds bad when you say it like that. But I knew guys — guys I served with who had it way worse than me. You see actual bad, and this doesn't... this isn't that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The guys you served with who had it worse — what ended up happening to them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Some of them... yeah. Some of them ended up bad. Lost jobs. Marriages fell apart. One guy — never mind. It's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to go there. But I noticed you went there for a second and then pulled back. That says something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I just don't want to end up like those guys. That's all I'm saying. I'm not saying I'm him. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet here you are. Something got you through that door today — and I don't think it was just someone telling you to show up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said... my wife said she was done. Not like, an empty threat done. She — she packed a bag. Took it to her mom's for a weekend. She came back but it was different after that. She looks at me different now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That must've been terrifying. Coming home and the bag's gone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I stood in the closet for I don't even know how long. I just stood there. I keep thinking, I've come back from worse than this — but I couldn't move. I couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's her name?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Diane. We've been married eight years. She kept everything together when I was deployed. Both times. She's... she's tougher than me, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You love her. That much is clear. And you're scared of losing her — not as some abstract possibility, but like it already happened once and you're still not over it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I survived two deployments. I don't... I'm not someone who falls apart. But losing her — losing my family over this? I can't. I can't let that happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a lot — deployment, coming home, trying to fit back into a life where the rules are completely different. You've been coping the best way you knew how. The fact that you're sitting here saying you're not willing to lose your family — that took something to say out loud. So what would it look like, if things were actually different six months from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just want her to look at me the way she used to. Before I came back and turned into... this. I want to be present. I'm physically in the room but I'm not — I'm somewhere else. My kids deserve better than that. I deserve better than that, I think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing from you today. You came in skeptical — you've been through counseling before, it hasn't stuck, and you're not sold on the idea that drinking is the problem. At the same time, something shifted when Diane packed that bag, and you haven't been able to shake it. You're not measuring yourself against hiding bottles anymore — you're talking about being present for your kids, being the person she married. You said "I deserve better than that" just now, and I don't think that was an accident. That's not nothing, Marcus. That's actually the start of something. I'd like to meet again if you're open to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, okay. I'm not saying I've got it all figured out or anything. But... maybe. I can come back.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Take your time getting settled. There's no rush here at all... I'm really glad you came in today. How are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I feel... I don't know. Ashamed, mostly. Coming here after — after everything. It's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It took something real to walk through that door today. When you say it's a lot — what's weighing on you most heavily right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had three years. Three years, you know? And then... I just... it all fell apart so fast. The drinking. I can't believe I'm back here. I can't believe I let myself end up back here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years of your life. And somewhere in you there's this sense that it just — slipped away. And now you're looking at where you are and it feels almost unbelievable to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Unbelievable is exactly the word. I wake up and I still think, like... how. How did I let that happen. I know better. I'm fifty years old, I've been through AA, I know what I'm supposed to do and I still just — I still did it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's real pain in that. I want to make sure I understand what was happening for you — the job loss. What was that like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Twenty-two years at the same company. Twenty-two years and they just... let me go. No warning, no real explanation, just, uh, here's your box, thanks for your service. And my whole — I mean my whole identity was wrapped up in that job. I didn't know who I was without it. I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. That wasn't just a job — that was a huge piece of how you understood yourself. And losing it that suddenly, with no real warning... that kind of loss can feel like the ground just drops out from under you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I — I tried. I swear I tried to hold it together. For a few months I was okay. But at some point I couldn't face another day sitting at home feeling useless. And I thought, just one drink. Just one. And... we all know how that goes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You tried to hold on, and eventually the pain got bigger than what you could carry alone. What scares you most now, when you look ahead?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I can't do it again. That I used up my one shot somehow. Three years felt like a miracle the first time. I don't know if — I'm fifty years old and I'm starting from zero. Again. I don't know if I have that in me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you got to three years — that didn't happen by accident. That came from something real inside of you. And you sitting here the day after finishing detox, rather than walking away and isolating... that says something too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I didn't want to waste any time. In detox, when I started to feel clearer, I just kept hearing my sponsor's voice. What he used to say. 'Don't pick up no matter what.' I didn't listen. But I kept hearing him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: His voice stayed with you, even through all of that. What was sobriety like during those three years — what did it actually give you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. Um... everything, really. I was present with my kids for the first time in years. Like actually present — I coached my son's baseball team one summer. I could look people in the eye. I didn't wake up every morning wondering what I'd said or done the night before. It was... it was a real life. A good one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were really there. With your kids, with yourself. A life where you weren't carrying that weight every single morning.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I threw that away. Or — I don't know. I don't want to say I threw it away. I got knocked down and I grabbed for the wrong thing. I don't know... maybe that's the same thing in the end.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It might be, or it might be an important distinction for you — and worth sitting with. What do you want now? If you could look six months ahead, what would you want your life to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sober. That's — first and foremost. I want to be able to call my kids without that knot in my stomach. Get back on my feet, find some kind of work. I don't need the big career anymore. I just want... something quiet and honest. Something I don't have to lie about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm hearing you right. You went through something devastating — losing a job that was central to who you were — and eventually the pain got too heavy to hold alone, and you reached for alcohol. And now you're here, clearer than you've been in months, and what's still alive in you is the memory of what sobriety gave you. Being present with your kids. Feeling like yourself. And a picture of something quieter and more honest going forward. Does that fit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that fits. When you put it like that... I don't know. It doesn't sound completely hopeless. Which is... it felt pretty hopeless in there. Most of last week felt pretty hopeless.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been to AA before — you had a sponsor, a community around you. What feels possible to you about reconnecting with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I need to. I already — I actually looked up meeting times last night on my phone. My old sponsor might still be around. I don't know if he'll still want to hear from me after... but. I think I need to try. AA was what made the difference the first time around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You looked up meeting times while you were still in detox. That's not a small thing. That's you reaching for something before you even had both feet on solid ground. That's the part of you that knows what it needs.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't thought of it that way. I just — I panicked. I didn't want to leave there and have nothing lined up. But yeah. Maybe that... maybe that means something. Maybe that's me not giving up on myself, even when I felt like I had.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It does mean something. What would feel like one doable step — just one — in the next few days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Call my sponsor. Or if he doesn't pick up, just go to a meeting. There's one Thursday nights about a mile from where I'm staying. I used to go to that one. I know a few of the guys there. I know they'd... they'd be glad to see me. Even now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've already got your eyes on Thursday night, a room with people who know you, and a sponsor you're willing to reach out to. You built three years once, and even at your lowest point in that detox room, something in you was already looking for the way back. I'm here with you in this. How are you feeling right now, compared to when you first walked in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Lighter. A little. Still scared, but... lighter. Like maybe I'm not just a guy who failed. Maybe I'm just — a guy who fell down and needs to get back up. I've done it before. Maybe I can do it again.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's good to see you back. I know last time felt a little... uncomfortable. How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I'm here, aren't I? My mom basically made me come again. It's whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up even when part of you really didn't want to. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I don't know. It just feels like everyone is acting like I, like, robbed a bank or something. I had two drinks at prom. Literally everyone was drinking. I just got caught.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel singled out. Like the reaction was way bigger than what actually happened. ... I also want to check in on something — your counselor mentioned some lab work came back from your recent physical. Can you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ugh. Yeah. My liver enzymes were elevated, or whatever. The doctor said it was 'concerning.' But she doesn't know me. She just sees like, numbers on a paper. It's probably nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
