utterances.text: That word — concerning — that had to land hard. Especially when it feels like nobody's really seeing the full picture of who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, I cried in the car after. Which is embarrassing. My mom completely freaked out and was like, 'I knew it, I knew it.' And I just wanted everyone to stop. It was a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You cried. So there was a moment where it actually got through. What was going through your mind in that car?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I kept thinking about my grandma. She had liver problems. And she died from it. So I had this like, one second where I was like — oh. And then I just pushed it down because I'm eighteen. It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your grandma.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. My family doesn't really talk about it but... she drank a lot. Like, a lot a lot. And I'm not like that. I would never get like that. I just — I'm not her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not becoming her — that really matters to you. You care deeply about that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Obviously. But like, drinking at parties isn't the same as what she did. Right? She was drinking alone, like every day. I'm not doing that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a difference that feels really important to you. I hear that. Can I ask — what do you picture for yourself, like, five years from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I got into State in the fall. I want to actually go, like, be somebody. Study something real. Get out of this town. I don't want to just... stay here and be nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to hold all of this together for a second. You've got this future you're moving toward — college, becoming someone you're proud of, getting out. And at the same time, there's a scary lab result, and a memory of your grandma that you pushed away but that clearly got to you. Those two things are living in the same person right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I never thought about it like that. Like two different... I don't know. It's weird to hear it out loud like that. I don't really want to think about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for that version of you — the one who gets to State, who builds something real — if drinking kept being part of the picture going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. Maybe nothing? But my friend Jake, he started drinking a lot junior year and he just, like, stopped caring about everything. Didn't even apply anywhere. I always kind of judged him for that. But now I'm like... was I doing the same thing? Am I?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to ask yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's kind of scary to say out loud. Like... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to say something that frightening out loud instead of pushing it back down. What does it feel like to actually hear yourself say it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Weird. Like... real? I usually just tell myself I'm fine and move on. But maybe I'm not totally fine. I don't know. Maybe I've just been saying that because it's easier.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted just now. What feels different from when you walked in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came in ready to like, argue with you again. But I'm kind of tired of arguing. I just... what if I actually let myself think about it? Like, do I even want drinking to be my thing? Because I don't know if I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to bring together everything you've shared today. You came back, even when it was hard. You got lab results that scared you more than you let anyone see. You thought about your grandma and felt something you've been carrying quietly. You've got a future at State that you really want. And just now, you said you're tired of arguing — and that you're not sure you even want this to be your thing. That's a lot of ground covered in one hour.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, I still don't think I'm like, some huge problem or whatever. But... I don't know. I think I actually want to talk about it. Like, actually talk. Not just defend myself the whole time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'd really like that too. And you get to set the pace — this is your space. If we came back to this next time, what would you want to start with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... why I actually drink. Like for real, not just 'because everyone does.' Because I don't totally believe that anymore. I think there's more to it.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Reyes. Make yourself comfortable... can I get you some water or anything before we get started?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, I'm good. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, I know walking into a place like this can feel a little... I don't know, maybe unfamiliar. What brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean... I saw something online. Like a flyer, kind of. I don't know, I've been thinking about some stuff lately. With drinking, mostly. I bartend, so it's like... it's everywhere for me. But something felt off recently and I figured, whatever, I'd come check this out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something felt off, and that was enough to get you through the door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess, yeah. It's not like I think I have a problem or whatever. Everyone at the bar drinks after shifts. It's kind of just... that's the culture, you know? You close down, you have a few, you decompress. It's pretty normal for the industry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's the norm where you work. And at the same time, something still made you want to come in. What was that something?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So... okay. This is gonna sound dumb. But a few weeks ago I was just like, lying in bed, and I started trying to think back — when was the last day I didn't drink? And I genuinely couldn't come up with one. Like, I went back three months in my head and just... nothing. Every single day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three months back, and not a single day you could find.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I mean — it's not like I'm blacking out every night. A couple drinks after a shift, that's it. But still. I don't know. I've been bartending four years. That's a long time without... a break, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four years is a long time. And even though you're telling yourself it makes sense — the job, the culture — that moment when you couldn't find the day still caught you off guard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. It did. I wasn't even trying to quit or anything, I was just curious. And then I couldn't do it. Couldn't find the day. And I don't know, that felt... weird. Like I didn't expect to feel weird about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The feeling surprised you more than the answer did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of, yeah. Like I'd been fine, I thought. But then that question just sat with me for days. I kept going back to it. Is this just... what my life is now? Every day, no exceptions? That feels weird to say out loud, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You let yourself sit with that question — that took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't really told anyone. All my friends are in the same scene so they'd just think I was being dramatic. Like, bro, you work at a bar, what did you expect. And I get that. But the thought keeps coming back, so... clearly some part of me isn't totally buying my own logic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying this mostly by yourself. What's it like, having that thought keep coming back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of heavy. Like I keep telling myself — it's fine, it's normal, it's a bartender thing. And then it's just... there again. I think part of me is worried. Not like, panicking. But... worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm getting this right. You came in on your own today — something you saw online nudged you, but the real thing was this moment a few weeks back where you looked for a day without drinking and couldn't find one going back months. You've been telling yourself it's just the job, it's what everyone does. But the thought keeps finding its way back, and part of you is worried. Does that sound close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's pretty much it. When you say it like that it sounds... I don't know. More real, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things were different — the way you'd actually want them to be — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just... I don't want to be 40 and still doing the exact same thing, you know? Like I want to actually choose to have a drink. Not just do it because the shift ended and that's what happens next. I want it to be a choice. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want it to feel like a choice again, not just something that happens automatically.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly that. Right now it just kind of... happens. The shift ends, I drink. Every time. And I don't even really decide to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know what you want it to feel like. That's not a small thing to know.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never really thought about it that way. I've just been focused on like, what's wrong with me. But yeah... I do know what I'd want it to look like. I hadn't framed it like that before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would feel like a good first step — something small, something that actually feels doable to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... try one day. See if I can do it. I honestly don't know if I can, which is kind of scary to admit out loud. But I think that's what I'd want to try first. Just one day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you walked in here today not really knowing what to expect, and you've landed somewhere real — that you want drinking to feel like a choice, not just something that runs on autopilot. And you've already got a first step in mind: one day, just to see. That's a meaningful place to be at the end of a first conversation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't totally know what comes next. But it feels like at least I'm not just ignoring it anymore. That feels better, I think.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know it takes... a lot, to walk through that door, especially after everything you've been through these past few weeks. How are you feeling right now — just, coming in here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really know why I'm here. My doctor set this up, so... I went through the detox thing and I'm out, so. I mean, I showed up, right? That's something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up. That matters. ... And it sounds like maybe part of you is still figuring out what this is all about — what you're even doing here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I'm not — I don't have like, a drinking problem the way people make it sound. I've been in the military, okay? Everybody drinks. It's just what you do after a deployment. It's how you decompress. I wasn't doing anything different than half the guys I served with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So in that world — the military world — it was just part of the culture. Normal. Expected, even.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Nobody pulled those guys aside and told them they had a problem. I did two deployments, I came back, I... you deal with stuff the way you know how. That's all it ever was. You come home and you're just trying to turn your brain off for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And you found a way to carry some really heavy things. Two deployments — that's not nothing. That kind of resilience is real. ... You mentioned your doctor referred you. What else, besides the doctor — what else is kind of pulling at you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... my wife. She, uh... she said some things. Before the detox. It got to me more than I expected it to. Which is — I don't know. I wasn't expecting that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something she said really landed. ... Even when part of you maybe didn't want it to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She had a bag packed. She wasn't even yelling, which was — that was somehow worse. She was just calm. And she said, 'I love you but I'm not watching you disappear.' Just... said it. Like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — her standing there, calm, a bag packed. What was going through your mind in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought she was bluffing. We've had fights before, so. But then I looked at her face and I just... yeah. She wasn't. And I didn't know what to do with that, so I went to my buddy's place and drank until I couldn't feel it anymore. Which I know is — yeah. I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You needed to make that feeling stop. ... And yet something brought you back. Something made you call the doctor, go through the detox. Something shifted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My son called me. He's eight. He just — 'Dad, when are you coming home?' That's all he said. And I couldn't answer him. I sat in my car for like an hour after that. I don't know. Something just... broke open.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your son's voice... broke something open in you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Yeah. I never wanted to be that guy, you know? The one who's never around, or who's around but you kinda wish he wasn't. My dad was like that. I swore I wouldn't be. I swore that for years and then I just... I became him anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that a long time — that image of the father you don't want to be. ... What kind of father do you want to be? For him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Present. Like, actually there. Not just in the house. My wife says even when I'm sober I'm somewhere else, and she's not — she's not wrong about that. I've been somewhere else for three years. Since I got back, really.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's something important here. You came in today not sure why you were here. But in just a little while you've told me that your wife is at a breaking point, that your son's voice cracked something open, and that you've known — for a while — that you've been somewhere else. There's real pain in all of that. And a lot of love too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... When you say it like that it sounds — I don't know. Heavy. It's heavy. I didn't think I was gonna, like, say all that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is heavy. And you've been carrying most of it alone, it sounds like. ... If you could see yourself six months from now — doing okay — what would that even look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't let myself think about that. Like, what does 'doing okay' even mean for someone like me? But... taking my kid to his games. Not counting drinks in my head. Actually being in a conversation with my wife without waiting for it to blow up. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being there. Really there. That's what you're describing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's all I want. I just... I don't know how to get from here to there. The detox — that was the hardest two weeks of my life, and I did two combat deployments. I didn't think I'd feel that sick. It scared me, honestly. Like, I didn't know my body needed it that bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You went through something physically brutal — and you didn't walk away from it. You stayed with it all the way through. That tells me something real about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I wasn't gonna quit. I'm stubborn, I guess. My wife says it's my worst quality. *short laugh* ... Maybe it can work for me sometimes instead of against me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Maybe it can. ... So thinking about the next few weeks — what feels like the most important thing you could do? Just one thing, if you had to name it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Talk to my wife. For real. Tell her I get it now — what I've been doing, what it's cost her. I think she deserves to actually hear that from me. And I want to pick my son up from school. Just... small stuff. But I want to start somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in today not sure why you were here. And now you're leaving having named the two people who matter most to you, what you actually want your life to feel like, and one real step you want to take. That's not nothing — that's real work. I'm glad you stayed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Me too, I think. I don't know if I'll — I mean, I'm not making any promises. But maybe I'll be back. That's more than I thought I'd say walking in here.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, have a seat wherever you're comfortable. I'm glad you made it today. How are you feeling after finishing the program?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Tired, mostly. Not great, if I'm being honest. But... I'm here, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You finished something really hard, and you still showed up this morning. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I kept thinking during the detox... why did I let it get that far? Like I knew. I knew it was getting bad and I just... kept going anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say you knew it was getting bad — what did that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't like... I wasn't drinking at nine in the morning or anything like that. It was evenings mostly. After Margaret passed, the evenings got real long. Real quiet. I'd have one to settle down and then... I don't know. One turned into more.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The evenings felt unbearable without her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We always watched the news together. Had dinner, watched the news, she'd fall asleep in her chair... and then she was just gone. And then I retired right around the same time, so it was like — everything just stopped. All at once.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's an enormous amount of loss hitting you at the same time. What did the drinking actually give you in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Quiet. It made the quiet... bearable. I know that probably sounds stupid to you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. It makes complete sense that you'd reach for something to soften that kind of pain.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The doctor scared me, I'll say that. Said my liver numbers were off. But I figured... I'm 65. What does it really matter at this point. I've had my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you wondered if there was even anything left worth protecting.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... my kids are grown, they've got their own lives. I don't really have a... I don't know what I have to get up for anymore. You know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet here you are — you finished the program, you walked in this door today. Something brought you here. What was it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My son called me. About a month ago. He was... he was crying. Said he couldn't just watch me do this to myself. I hadn't heard him cry like that since... well, since his mother's funeral. That got to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It took a lot to actually hear that from him. And it sounds like your relationship with your son — that means everything to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's all I've got, really. Him and the grandkids. But I think... I think they started keeping their distance. And I can't blame them, honestly. I wasn't — I wasn't showing up the way a father should.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you to have them closer again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. Those grandkids... God, they grow up so fast. I missed my grandson's birthday last year. I was... I wasn't in good shape. He's six. He doesn't understand why grandpa didn't come. I told myself I'd make it up to him but... I don't know if I did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, make sure I've got it right. You lost Margaret and your sense of purpose at nearly the same time, and drinking became the only way to get through those long, quiet evenings alone. The doctor's warning registered, but it was really your son — hearing him cry — and missing that birthday... those were the things that moved you to actually do something. And underneath all of it, you're still a man who loves his family deeply and hasn't stopped wanting to be there for them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. When you say it like that it doesn't sound like I'm just some — some sad old drunk. There was a reason it happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a story behind it. And you're here trying to write a different one.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to. I really do. I just... sometimes I get scared I'm too old to change. Or that the damage is already done and I'm just going through the motions.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would change actually look like for you — not in some big abstract way, just in a regular Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... calling my son more. Not waiting for him to call me. And I used to do woodworking — haven't touched it in years. I'd like to get back to that. And honestly just... not feeling ashamed when he comes by. That'd be enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those are real, specific things. And the fact that you can name them — the woodworking, the calls, feeling like yourself again around your son — that tells me a lot about who you still are underneath all of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to be pretty good at it, actually. Made a rocking chair once, took me about six months. Margaret used to sit in it out on the porch in the summer. Still there. My son has it now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That chair is still in the family. And maybe part of what we're working toward — together, over these sessions — is finding your way back to the man who had the patience and the skill to make something like that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd like that. I really would. I think... yeah. I think I'm ready to actually try this time.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You seemed... different when you walked in today. Like you were carrying something heavy before you even sat down. What's been going on since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't really want to do this today, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not sure this is worth your time right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I had a bad week, okay? I don't need to sit here and have someone pick apart every single thing I do. I'm not — I'm not some case study.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something happened this week that really got to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My department head called me in. Someone said something — I don't even know who — and now there's this whole... I have to meet with HR next week. So yeah. Great week. Really.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds humiliating. Being called in, not knowing who said what, now facing HR... that's a lot of exposure all at once. Especially for someone who's spent years building a reputation at that school.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Humiliating is a word for it, yeah. I've given twelve years to that place. Twelve years. And now I'm — what, I'm some kind of liability? That's how they see me now?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ... Twelve years. That means something to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Of course it does. I'm good at my job. I know I am. The kids — they actually come to me with stuff. Real stuff. Not because they have to. I'm not some... I'm not a bad person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nobody here is saying you're a bad person. And I can hear how much you care about those kids — that's real, that's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Then why does it feel like that's exactly what everyone thinks? Like I'm some drunk stumbling through the hallways? I show up. Every day. I do my job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Showing up — being reliable, being present — that's a core part of how you see yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. And I... okay. Fine. I know this week wasn't — I know I wasn't at my best. I know that. But I'm not... it's not like I'm falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: This week was harder than most.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I drank more than I should have. After the meeting with Greenberg, I just — I went home and I had more than I meant to. And the next morning was rough. And I... look, I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew it was too much, even as it was happening.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe not in the moment. The next morning, yeah. I was sitting in my car in the parking lot just trying to... trying to hold it together enough to walk in. And I kept thinking — what am I doing? Like, what am I actually doing?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "What am I doing." ... What do you think you were really asking yourself with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. It's like... I know this isn't sustainable. I'm not an idiot, I know that. But knowing something and actually doing something about it — those are completely different things, and I don't know why I can't just...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a gap between knowing and being able to move. And you've been living in that gap for a while. That's an exhausting place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is exhausting. I'm tired of — pretending I'm fine all day and then going home and... and the thing is, I don't even enjoy it anymore. That's the part that gets me. I don't. It's just what I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not giving you anything anymore. It's just... something to get through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. It started after my divorce. It was like, okay, this is how I get to sleep, this is how I stop thinking about everything I screwed up. And then it just — it became the thing. Every night. Just there, waiting for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can trace it back. You know exactly where it came from and why it made sense at the time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do. And that's the weird part — I know why I started, I know it's become a problem, I know what it's costing me. I just... I don't know who I am at night without it. That probably sounds insane.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound insane at all. It sounds like you've been carrying something really painful for a very long time, and this became the only way you knew how to put it down for a few hours. Of course it filled that space.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my job. I don't want my students to... they look at me a certain way. Like I'm someone solid. Someone they can count on. And I want to keep being that for them. I really do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's still something worth fighting for here. Who you are in that classroom, what those kids see in you — that matters enough that you're sitting in this chair today, even though part of you walked in wanting to walk right back out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I don't know what the next step looks like. But I think I might actually need real help. Not just — not just talking. Like, actual help.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know you mentioned at the front desk you were short on time, so I really appreciate you taking a few minutes. Can you tell me a little about what brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I saw the flyer out front, and I thought maybe — look, I'm not sure this is even the right place. I'm 55. Everyone out there in that waiting room is like, what, 20? It just feels a little ridiculous, honestly. I don't know why I didn't just keep walking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not sure this is the right fit — and yet something made you stop.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I was dropping something off for my daughter, she's a student here, and I saw the flyer about alcohol and I just... I don't know. I almost left three times in the waiting room too, so. I'm not even sure what I'm doing here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about that flyer made you pause, even after almost leaving three times. What do you think that was?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. I guess because I've been drinking more than I should. Or — more than usual, anyway. It's been a rough year. A really rough year.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A really rough year.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My husband passed. Eight months ago. Heart attack — completely out of nowhere. And I just... yeah. I started drinking more after. Which, I mean... who wouldn't, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a profound loss. I'm sorry. When you say you've been drinking more than usual — what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: A glass of wine with dinner kind of turned into, um... a bottle. Sometimes more. It's mostly at night when the house is quiet. It's honestly the only time I can actually sleep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying something enormous, and the fact that you walked through that door today — that takes something real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Look, it's probably not even a real problem, okay? I'm still functioning. I go to work, I pay my bills. I'm not — I mean, I'm not some kind of alcoholic. I don't want you to think that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to be clear — you're managing, keeping things together. That matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. My friends have basically disappeared — Carol hasn't called in two months, Margaret even longer. My kids are busy. I'm not bothering anyone. I just have wine at night by myself. That's what grown adults do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned the house gets very quiet at night. What goes through your mind in those moments — before the wine?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... that's when it hits you. During the day you can stay busy, keep moving. But at night the bed just feels... I kept his pillow on his side for three months. I still talk to him sometimes. Out loud. Which probably sounds completely crazy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound crazy at all. It sounds like you miss him terribly — and the drinking quiets that pain just enough to get through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. And I know it's not a solution. I'm not stupid. I know that. But everything else feels like too much. Talking to people, going through his things... I just can't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand what you've shared. You lost your husband eight months ago, and the grief is still very raw. The nights are the hardest. The drinking helps you get through them. And at the same time, some part of you was worried enough about it that when you saw that flyer today, you didn't keep walking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. That's pretty much it. I don't want to be this person. I didn't — this isn't who I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Who were you before?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had friends. Real ones. I used to host these big Sunday dinners — my daughter would bring her roommates, the whole house full. I had a garden. I took a pottery class on Thursday nights. I don't do any of that anymore. But the strange thing is... I miss her. I miss the person I was, and I can't find her anywhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's still there. You just described her in detail. And underneath all of this grief, it sounds like you genuinely want to find your way back to her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. Maybe. My daughter keeps asking me to come to Sunday brunch with her friends, and I keep saying no, but... maybe I should say yes sometime. I don't know. It feels scary. Everything feels scary now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sitting here and saying out loud — 'I miss who I was, I want to find her again' — that's not a small thing. That's actually something really important to know about yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never said that out loud before. I keep telling everyone I'm fine. My son calls every Sunday and I say, oh I'm fine, everything's fine. I'm not fine. I don't think I've been fine in a long time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Now that you've said it out loud — what feels like even one small step that might feel right for you, going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd like to actually talk to someone. Properly, I mean. Not just, um, dropping in between picking up my daughter's jacket. Someone who could help me figure out the drinking, but also just... all of it. Because I think they're the same thing, aren't they.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like today you walked in not quite knowing why — and you're leaving knowing something really important. That the drinking and the grief are connected. That you're not okay, and it's okay to say that. And that you want support finding your way back to yourself. I'd like to connect you with one of our counselors for ongoing sessions. How does that feel?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It feels... yeah. Good, actually. I didn't expect to feel good walking out of here. I thought I'd just grab a pamphlet and pretend it never happened.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today... I know you mentioned you're between classes so I want to make sure we use this however feels most useful to you. How are you doing right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... fine. I'm here, right? That counts for something, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like showing up today wasn't the easiest thing. What's it been like this past week or so?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I know why I'm here. The court thing. I just... I don't really see how talking about it is going to do anything. I teach kids, I handle things. This was just a bad night. One bad night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A bad night that felt pretty separate from who you really are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. I'm not — I mean, I'm a teacher. I go in every single day. I coach the after-school debate team. I'm not some... I don't know what they think I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear how much being a teacher is part of who you are. And I'm curious — what does a typical evening look like for you, once you get home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I come home, I... I have a drink. Decompress. Maybe two. I deal with thirty twelve-year-olds all day, so — you need something to take the edge off. Everyone does something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's become the thing at the end of the day that makes it all feel manageable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And I know what you're going to say. But it's not like I'm sitting there drinking a bottle of vodka. It's a few beers. Maybe some wine. That's... normal. Plenty of people do this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a lot — the job, thirty kids every day, this legal thing on top of it. And you're still showing up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know how much longer I can, though. My department head has been giving me these looks. And then a colleague pulled me aside last week and I just... I wanted to disappear. Like, is that what I've become?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment with your colleague — can you tell me a little more about what that was like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Embarrassing. Just... humiliating. She was kind about it, which almost made it worse somehow. She said she was worried and I just stood there and I didn't even know what to say. Because part of me knows she's not wrong. But another part just wanted to tell her to mind her own business.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you recognized something true in what she was saying... and sitting with that part is really hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I don't know. I've been doing this for years and nothing bad has really happened. Until now. And I just keep thinking — like, is this who I am now? Is this just... it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you ask 'is this it' — what are you afraid the answer might be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I already know the answer. That... I've been telling myself it's fine for so long I stopped actually checking. I used to be really present, you know? Like, the kind of teacher who remembered stuff — kids' birthdays, what they were going through at home. Now I just... get through the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That connection with your students — being really present for them — it sounds like that's something you genuinely valued, and you feel like you've been losing it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My best student this year, Marcus. Smart kid. He asked me last month if I was okay. Fourteen years old, asking me that. I laughed it off but... I thought about it the whole drive home. And then I had three drinks instead of two.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You came in today because you had to — but there's a part of you that a fourteen-year-old saw clearly, that's been paying attention. You feel like you've drifted from the person you were. The drinking started as a way to manage real pressure, and somewhere along the way it shifted into something that's quietly costing you things that matter to you. Does that feel close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — I don't love hearing it out loud. But yeah. That's pretty close.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I wonder — if things were genuinely different a year from now, what would you want that to look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want to not dread Mondays. I'd want to actually sleep — like real sleep. I wake up feeling like garbage most days and I've just... accepted that. I don't think I should have to accept that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there — deciding you don't have to accept feeling like garbage — that's not a small thing. That's you saying you deserve more than this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Yeah, I do. I just haven't really thought about it like that. I've been so busy making excuses I forgot I was the one losing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were working so hard to protect the image — the teacher who's handling it, the guy who's fine — that the cost sort of crept up on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My therapist in college — god, I haven't thought about her in years — she used to say the story we tell to survive sometimes becomes the cage. I think... that's kind of where I am. That's exactly where I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here rushed, maybe a little reluctant. And somewhere in the middle of all this you found something real — a version of yourself that wants to feel present again, wants to be the teacher Marcus sees when he asks if you're okay. I don't want to rush past that. What feels like a next step — even a small one — that you'd actually be willing to take?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... coming back. Talking again. I don't know if I'm ready to say out loud that I have a problem. But I think I'm ready to stop pretending I definitely don't.

client_context: A 37-year-old middle school teacher who drinks every evening and occasionally comes to work hungover. A colleague noticed and expressed concern privately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came in today. I know this kind of first step... it takes something. Why don't we just start wherever feels right for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... I don't really know how to do this. My friend Marcus, he kind of... he sat me down last week and said he was worried. And I figured, you know, just to show him I'm taking it seriously.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So Marcus reached out, and part of you wanted to honor that. What was that conversation like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It felt like an ambush. I mean, he's my friend so I know he meant well, but... I'm a functioning adult. I have a job, I show up, I pay my bills. I don't really know what he thinks he saw.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like things are under control — and then your friend says he's worried, and that just doesn't fit with how you see yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean... I have a beer or two after work. That's not a crime. Half of America does that. My dad did that. It's just... it's just how you decompress.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that decompressing. What do your evenings actually look like when you get home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home, I change, I... usually crack one open while I'm making dinner. Watch something. Have a few more. Nothing crazy. I'm in bed by eleven, up by six. I function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've built a kind of rhythm around it. It helps you shift gears after what sounds like a genuinely demanding day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Teaching middle school is... look, I don't know if you've been around twelve and thirteen year olds lately, but it's a lot. Emotionally it's just — there's always something. Some kid crying, some parent emailing you at eight PM. I need that off switch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That off switch matters a lot to you. And I'm curious... if some part of you wasn't at least a little concerned, would you have come in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know. Maybe not. There have been some mornings where I've just — I showed up and I wasn't totally there. And the kids notice stuff. They're perceptive at that age. I don't love that feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's something that sits with you about those mornings. That gap between the teacher you are and the one you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I... yeah. I have this one student, Darius. Real rough situation at home, and he's actually started to trust me. He comes in early sometimes just to hang out in the classroom. And I've had a couple mornings where I'm going through the motions, I'm not sharp. And I think about him sitting there and I just... that bothers me. That really bothers me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would you want Darius to see when he looks at you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who's got it together. Someone who shows up. That's the whole point, you know? I had a teacher like that when I was his age. That's why I became a teacher — I wanted to be that for somebody else. And now I'm sitting here worried that I'm... not being that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that Darius comes in early just to be near you... that says something real about who you are to him, even on the hard days.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I hope so. I just... I don't want to blow it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does blowing it look like to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... becoming someone I don't recognize. My dad drank. Not just a little. And I swore I wouldn't — I told myself I was different. I have a degree, I have a career, I'm not him. But lately I'm like... am I? Is this how it starts? Because I don't know when a few beers became more than a few. I genuinely don't know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been holding this fear very quietly. That maybe the thing you promised yourself you'd never become... might be closer than you want to admit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I don't say that out loud. I've never said that to anyone. It's... yeah. It's scary. I don't really know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold a few things together that you've shared with me. You came in partly for Marcus, but also because something in you knew you needed to. You love what you do, you care deeply about kids like Darius, and that version of yourself — the teacher who's fully there — matters to you more than almost anything. And at the same time, you've started to notice the drinking getting between you and that person. And underneath all of that, there's this quiet fear that you might be walking a road you've watched someone else walk before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's exactly it. I don't know if I've ever heard it laid out like that. It's actually kind of a relief? Like, to just say it? I thought coming in here I'd feel like I was confessing something. But I just feel like... I don't know. Like maybe something can actually change.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would change look like for you? If things were genuinely different a year from now — what would you want that to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to come home and not immediately go for the fridge. I want to have a bad day and just... sit with it instead of numbing it. I want to show up for Darius sharp. And honestly — I want to not be scared of myself anymore. That's probably the big one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today protecting yourself, and somewhere in the last hour you told me the truest thing about yourself. That takes real courage. I don't say that lightly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel courageous. I feel terrified. But... less terrified than I did an hour ago. That's something, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It really is. Before we wrap up today — what feels like the smallest possible next step that would still mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... coming back. Talking to someone again. I think I've been alone with this for a really long time. And I didn't realize until just now how much that was part of the problem.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Derek. Fair warning, that chair has a slight lean to the left — I keep meaning to fix it but... haven't. You want anything? Water, coffee I can't actually promise is good?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, no, I'm good. Thanks. [looks around] So this is — yeah. Okay. I wasn't really sure what to expect, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk-ins are always a little like that, right? You're here and you're not totally sure how you ended up here. So — what's on your mind? What made today the day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My boss, basically. There was a... situation at work. I got sent here. Or like, it was 'strongly suggested.' [air quotes] So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Got it. So part of you is here because someone else wanted you here. And yet — you showed up. That's actually not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I didn't want to lose my job, so. [shrugs] I've done therapy before. Didn't really go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, that tracks. What happened with the therapy before? What made you walk away from it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The guy just kept, like... asking how I felt about my mom. And I'm thinking, I'm here about drinking, not — you know. It felt useless. Like I was wasting time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it felt off-target. Like he had his agenda and you had yours, and they were just... not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And then I just stopped going. [pause] Which, I know, doesn't look great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I appreciate you being upfront about that. So help me understand — when you say drinking, what does that actually look like for you right now? Just your average week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it depends. Some days nothing. Some days more than I should. I'm not like — I'm not a morning drinker, I don't drink at work. The thing at work was a one-time thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're making sure I know it's not out of control. How you're seen — that matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. I've worked that job for nine years. I'm not some — yeah. [gets quieter] But the last few months have been... rough. Like actually rough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nine years. That's a lot to protect.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I built that. From nothing. And now my boss is looking at me like I'm a liability, and I'm sitting in a — no offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: None taken. This room has seen better days and I'm aware. [pause] But — nine years, building something from nothing, and now you're scared it might slip away. That sounds exhausting. What's been driving the rough few months?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Everything? [long pause] My dad died last fall. And I just... I didn't really deal with it. I just kept going. You know how you do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You lost him, and you just... kept moving. Didn't let yourself stop.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [voice drops] He and I weren't even that close. Which almost makes it worse, I think. Like I'm grieving something that never happened, not something I actually had. That sounds stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. Grieving the relationship you never got to have — that's a real loss, maybe one of the harder kinds. And you've been carrying that — along with the depression, the job stress — and the drinking has been... what? Quieting things down a little?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [exhales slowly] It's like it turns the volume down. At night especially. I can't sleep otherwise. I know it's not — I know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know. [gently] What do you know?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That it's probably making the depression worse. I've read stuff. I just... it's the only thing that actually works, and I don't have a better thing yet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not in denial. You're in a bind — and those are actually two very different things. You know what the cost is, and you're using it anyway because right now it's the only tool in the box that works even a little. That makes sense. It's not weakness. It's someone doing the best they can with what they've got.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Huh. [small pause] Nobody's ever put it like that. Usually I just get the speech about my liver.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hard to compete with a good liver speech. [smiles] But seriously — if we could actually work on finding some of those other tools, and you didn't have to white-knuckle it alone at 11 PM... what would better even look like for you? What does that feel like in your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... sleeping. Actually sleeping. Not having that weight in my chest every morning. And going into work and having my boss look at me like I'm the guy he hired. Because I used to be pretty good at that job. I want to be that guy again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still are that guy. He's just been dealing with a lot, mostly by himself, for a long time. [pause] Here's what I heard today: you lost your dad and you're carrying grief that's complicated and messy. You've got depression that hasn't been properly treated. You've been using alcohol to manage pain that is very real. And underneath all of that, there's someone who built a nine-year career from the ground up and still cared enough to walk through that door today. That's not a liability. That's someone worth working with. So — you want to give this one a real shot?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [quiet nod] Yeah, I think... I want to try. For real this time.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come in, please. Make yourself comfortable wherever you'd like to sit. I'm glad you found your way here today. What brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I almost didn't come. I saw something online about this place and I figured... I don't know, whatever, why not. But I'll tell you right now — I've done therapy before and it was completely pointless. So I'm not walking in here with a lot of hope.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're walking in the door already expecting this to go nowhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. Last guy I saw just kept wanting to talk about my mom and my feelings and all that. Didn't help anything. I still went home and drank. So. That's... that was a fun six sessions.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking is still happening. What do you think is going on with that — not your sister's take, not your doctor's — yours. What's your read on it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: From my perspective? I drink because it helps. That's it. Everyone acts like I'm some kind of... like there's something broken about me. But I function. I go to work, I pay my bills, I'm not passed out in a ditch. So I don't really get what the big problem is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding it together. And drinking is part of how that happens.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And look — I've been depressed since my twenties. Like, diagnosed, actual clinical depression. I tried the meds, three different ones. Tried the exercise thing, the journaling, whatever. The alcohol actually works. Like it genuinely helps. So maybe instead of telling me to stop the one thing that works, people should figure out why nothing else does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been at this a long time. Trying things. Not just giving up and lying down. That takes something out of a person — years of fighting something that doesn't quit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know if I'd call it fighting. I'm just tired, honestly. I'm genuinely exhausted. And every time I try something new it's like — great, another thing that doesn't work, add it to the list. At some point you just stop adding things to the list.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That exhaustion — what does a regular day look like for you? Just a Tuesday, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Wake up. Already feel like garbage before I've done anything. Go to work — that part's actually okay, keeps me busy. Come home. Maybe eat something. And then yeah, I'll have a few drinks. Watch something. Fall asleep. And then do it again. That's... that's basically every day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You wake up already carrying something heavy. Make it through the day. And then the drinks are the one part where you're not just grinding through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's like... it's the only point in my day where I'm not white-knuckling everything. I can just sit there and things don't feel so... heavy. For like two, three hours. And then I go to sleep and it starts over. But those hours — I don't know. That's what I've got.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those few hours where things aren't so heavy... what would it mean to you if you could have more of that? Without it depending on the alcohol to get there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I mean obviously that would be better. But here's the thing — I've never actually had that. Even before I was drinking like this, I was just miserable. So I don't really know what that would even look like. I've never had a version of my life where I felt okay and didn't have to work that hard for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not sure there's a version of this where you feel okay and it doesn't cost something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah, that's actually exactly it. I've just always assumed that feeling like this is the deal. Like this is just me. Some people have good lives and some people have this. I'm in the second category.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm getting this right. You've been living with depression since your twenties. You've tried a lot of things — meds, other approaches — and nothing's really stuck. Drinking gives you relief, even if it's temporary. You tried therapy before and it didn't help, which is a big part of why you almost didn't come today. But you did come. And underneath all the skepticism, there's someone who's exhausted from the same day, every day. Does that sound close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's about right. I don't even know why I came, honestly. Maybe just... I don't know. I got sick of the routine. Something needed to be different, even if I don't think it will be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If this were to actually help — and I'm not promising anything, I just want to know what you'd want — what would that look like for you eventually?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'd want to feel less terrible. That's not complicated. Like just... getting up in the morning and not immediately feeling like it's too much. And I've been isolating a lot these past few years. I don't really talk to anyone. I'd want that to change, maybe. Actually have some kind of — I don't know. Life outside of work and the couch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not just saying 'stop drinking.' You're talking about something bigger — actually feeling different in the morning, being connected to people again. That's not a small thing to name.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess so. I never really... I always just thought about the drinking as the problem but when you put it like that, it's like — yeah. The drinking is probably making everything else worse at this point. Like I know that logically. I'm not an idiot. But knowing something and actually changing it are two very different things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned you've been isolating. Is there anyone — or anything — in your life right now that you actually care about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dog. Which is embarrassing to say but... yeah. And my sister. She drives me absolutely crazy but she's the one who kept pushing me to do something about all this. She's called me at the right time more than once, if you know what I mean. I've never actually told her that. But yeah. Those are the two.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She keeps showing up. Even when it's hard. And somewhere in you, you feel that — even if saying it out loud is difficult.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I do. I just... I'm sick of being the person she has to worry about. That's actually probably more of why I'm here than anything else I've said. I don't want to be a burden on her anymore. I'm almost forty years old and my sister is still checking in to make sure I'm okay. That's... that's not right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really important thing you just said. You don't want to keep being someone she has to carry. So I want to ask — not about everything, just about next week. What would one small step look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd... I'd come back. That's probably the step, right? I'm not going to promise you anything dramatic. I'm not going to say I'm throwing out all the bottles tonight or whatever. But I can come back next week. I can do that.

client_context: A 39-year-old diagnosed with depression who self-medicates with alcohol. Has tried therapy before and dropped out. Skeptical but willing to give it one more try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining me today, Marcus. I know you're at home, so hopefully that makes things at least a little more comfortable. I want you to know there's no agenda on my end — no checklist I'm trying to get through. We can go at whatever pace works for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I'm only here because HR told me I had to be. So... let's just get this over with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. And I appreciate you being straight with me about that — genuinely. Can you tell me what happened, from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What happened is my boss completely overreacted. I had a couple drinks at lunch, came back, and apparently that's some huge deal now. I've been at that company six years. Six years. And suddenly I'm the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Six years of showing up, and this one thing feels like it's erased all of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like none of it matters anymore. And now I gotta come talk to a therapist like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's embarrassing, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Coming here wasn't your choice, and there's this feeling of being reduced to just one moment after six years. I'm curious — what would you want me to know about you that your HR file doesn't capture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm a good worker. I'm good at my job. Things have been rough at home and I deal with it how I deal with it, and that's always been my business. Or at least it used to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Things have been rough, and drinking is how you've been getting through it. And it felt like your own business — until now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And I'm not gonna sit here and lie to you — I drink. Okay? But I'm not some... I function. I go to work. I pay my bills. I'm not the guy passed out in a ditch somewhere.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not in denial — you're saying you can see what's happening, you just don't think it's as serious as everyone's making it out to be. What does a typical week actually look like for you, if you don't mind me asking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... a few beers after work most nights. More on weekends. When I can't sleep I'll have a couple more. It helps with the — I have depression, been dealing with it for years. The medication made me feel like a zombie, so I stopped. The drinking kind of takes the edge off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You figured out what helped you feel something other than that flat, zombie feeling. And honestly — a lot of people in that situation just stop functioning entirely. You kept going.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. I kept going. I'm still here... I just — I'm tired. I'm really tired of feeling like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does tired look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like waking up and already being done with the day before it's even started. And I know the drinking doesn't actually fix anything, like I know that, but for a few hours I'm not thinking about all of it. The job stuff, my ex... I have a daughter. She's eight. I don't see her as much as I used to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your daughter.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Her mom and I split two years ago and I — I don't always show up the way I should. And she notices. Eight-year-olds notice everything. And I don't want to be that guy. That's not who I wanted to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Who did you want to be — for her?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone she could count on. My dad wasn't around. Like, at all. And I always told myself I'd be different. And now I'm sitting here wondering... am I actually different? Because from the outside maybe it doesn't look that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure I've got it right. You've been carrying a lot — depression that was never treated in a way that actually worked for you, pressure at work, the split with your daughter's mom, not seeing her as much as you want. You found something that took the edge off all of that. But now it's starting to cost you things you actually care about. And underneath everything, there's a person who really doesn't want to become his father. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's — I didn't think about it all together like that but... yeah. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took guts to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've done therapy twice before. Stopped both times. I just — is it actually possible for someone like me to get better? Because honestly, I've kind of stopped believing that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real question and I don't want to just hand you a pep talk. So let me ask — what would better actually look like, for you specifically?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Getting through a week without feeling like I need a drink to survive it. Picking my daughter up on Saturday and not being ashamed of myself when I drop her off. Maybe figuring out the depression without feeling like a vegetable. I don't know. That sounds like a lot when I say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like a life that has room in it. Room for her, room for you to feel things without being completely overwhelmed by them. That's not vague — that's actually really clear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't let myself think about what I actually want in... I don't know how long. Usually I'm just trying to get through the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here's where we are. You came in today because you had to, and you've been skeptical — which makes complete sense given your history with therapy. But something happened in this conversation. You talked about your daughter, about who you wanted to be, about what's exhausting you. None of that came from me. That came from you. I don't think you've given up — not completely. And I'd like to keep talking, if you're open to it. Not to fix you. Just to help you figure out what you want and what might actually get you there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Okay. I'll come back. I'm not making any promises but — yeah. I'll come back.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today, Harold. I know this isn't a small thing — coming here right after finishing the program. There's no agenda on my end. I just want to understand where you're at. How are you feeling today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... okay, I guess. Tired, mostly. They kept us pretty busy in there, which was probably the point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was the experience like for you — going through the detox program?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hard. Some days were real hard. But I finished it, so... I don't know. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You finished it. That's not nothing — a lot of people don't make it through, especially after decades of a different kind of life.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'd call it... I mean, my daughter basically showed up at my door and said she wasn't leaving without me. I didn't fight her on it. I was just too tired to fight, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like part of you was ready — even if it took her showing up to make it real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know. I look at myself and I think... is this who I am now? Just sitting in that house, alone, drinking? My wife passed four years ago and I just... it sort of snuck up on me. The whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that — how it snuck up on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I retired, and at first it was fine. Felt like a vacation. Then Margaret died, and the days just got... long. I'd have a beer in the afternoon just to have something to do. Then two. Then it wasn't beer anymore. I wasn't — I wasn't hurting anyone. I was just in my house.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The loneliness crept in, and the drinking kind of filled that space where your routine used to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And then my doctor — Dr. Patel — he said my liver enzymes were all elevated. Said if I kept going I was looking at serious damage down the road. That scared me, if I'm honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What went through your mind when he told you that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought about my kids. My grandkids. I thought... I don't want to be a cautionary tale. I've already missed enough. I missed my son's promotion dinner because I was — I was in no shape to go. Three months ago. I still can't look him in the eye about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment — missing his dinner — it still sits with you. Like something you can't put down.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It does. It really does. I used to be... I was a good father. I coached little league. I showed up. And somewhere along the way I just... stopped. I don't know when exactly, but I stopped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that it still bothers you — that you hold yourself to that standard of being present — that tells me something real about who you are, underneath all of this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel like that person right now. But I want to. I think... that's actually why I'm here. Not just because of my daughter or my liver enzymes. Because I miss being someone. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes a lot of sense. Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You've been through real losses — Margaret, your sense of purpose after retiring — and drinking became the way to get through the long days. But over time it cost you things that matter: your health, moments with your family, and your sense of yourself as the father and grandfather you want to be. And now, coming out of the program, something in you is saying — I want to find my way back to that person. Is that close?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I didn't think I'd say all that out loud, but... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — being that person again? If things were going well six months from now, what would be different about your days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd be at my grandson's baseball games. Sober. Actually watching, not just... sitting there. I'd call my son more. I'd get out of the house. Maybe have something to do in the mornings that means something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can picture it pretty clearly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I can. And that's... that's new, actually. A month ago I couldn't picture anything past the next afternoon.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something's shifted for you. Given everything you've described — the loneliness, needing structure, needing people — what do you think is one thing that would actually help you build toward that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There's a men's group at my church. I never went because I thought it was — I don't know, not really my thing. But maybe it's time. I need people around me. Real people, not just the TV.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know what you need and you already know where to find it. That's a real insight, Harold.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just have to walk through the door. That's always the hard part for me. But... I walked through this door today, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You really did. And I want you to hold onto that. You came in today — still fragile, right out of a hard program — and you talked honestly about your wife, your son, your health, and the person you want to be again. That takes courage. Before we wrap up, I'd like to schedule our next session, and I want to suggest that the church group becomes a concrete goal we track together. How does that sound to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Good. Yeah. I'd like that. I think... I think I'm actually ready to try this time. Not just going through the motions.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you, Marcus. Come on in... How have things been going since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: You really wanna know? Same as always. I'm here because I have to be, not because I want to be. Let's just get that straight right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. You're clear about that — being here isn't your choice, and that sits wrong with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sits wrong. Yeah, you could say that. I lost three days of work last month just showing up to these... sessions. Three days. You know what that costs me? And for what? To talk about my feelings?

utterances.speaker: therapist
