utterances.text: That's a real cost. Time, money, your job on the line... You mentioned last time things had been going better. I'm wondering what happened this week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I slipped up, alright? I had a few drinks. It's not like I went on some bender or whatever. Things got stressful at home and I had a couple beers. That's it. I'm not gonna pretend it didn't happen but it's also not... it's not what you're probably thinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Things piled up at home, and you found yourself reaching for a drink.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife's been on my case constantly. Between her and the court and my boss watching everything I do, it's like... I can't breathe. A beer is the only thing that shuts everything out for five minutes. Is that so hard to understand?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like you're surrounded on all sides and there's just nowhere to go... What's been happening at home, if you're okay talking about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She found some receipts. From a bar. Two weeks ago. I only had like two, three drinks, I drove home fine, but she acted like I'd... I don't know. Like I'm a complete failure. Like that's all I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She reacted strongly, and that landed hard. Like no matter what you do, she only sees the worst.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She doesn't trust me. And I get it, I guess... after everything. But I've been trying. I actually have been trying. And she just — she doesn't see that. She only ever sees the screw-ups.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you knows she has reasons to worry, and at the same time you're exhausted that the effort isn't getting seen. What does the trying look like? What have you actually been doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't drink for three weeks straight. That's... that's not nothing. I've been going to work every day, not calling in sick like I used to. I've been picking my son up from school twice a week. Those are real things. Those count.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those are real things. Three weeks without drinking. Showing up to work. Being there for your son. You did those things.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And then one bad night and it's like none of it counts. I'm just... I'm tired of feeling like I can never win. Like no matter what I do it's never gonna be enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm getting the whole picture... You came in today carrying a lot. The court, your boss, your wife — it feels like pressure from every direction. You had a slip after three solid weeks of doing things differently. And underneath all of it there's this fear that the ground just keeps shifting, that it'll never be enough. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's kind of exactly it. I don't usually think about it like that but... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm curious about that three-week stretch. What was different then? What made it possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think I was scared. After the last court date, the judge was real clear — one more thing and I'm looking at actual jail time. That scared me more than I let on. So I just told myself, one day at a time. Don't touch it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fear woke something up in you. And you used it — you made it work for three whole weeks.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But then that one night everything piled up and I... I didn't even think about it. I just did it. Like autopilot. And after — I felt kind of sick about it. Like, what's the point of all that work if I'm just gonna blow it anyway?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That you felt sick about it — that matters. That's not nothing. That's a part of you that cares about what you're building.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I do care. My son's eight. I don't want him to think this is just... who his dad is. I want him to see something different. I used to think that was just something people said, you know, 'do it for the kids.' But lately it's... it's real to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like for him to see you differently?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Him not being embarrassed. Not having to explain to his friends why his dad couldn't show up to stuff. I want to be at his games, his school things. Sober. Actually present — not just physically there, you know? That's... that's something I actually want. For real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being truly present for him. That's what matters most to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I know I got a long way to go. I'm not gonna sit here and pretend I've got it figured out. But maybe... maybe it's not totally hopeless? I don't know. The slip messed me up but I still came back here. That's something, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is something. You slipped, and you still came in. You talked honestly about what happened instead of just going through the motions. You have a reason that's real to you — your son, being present, not just showing up. And you've already shown yourself, three weeks at a time, that you can do this. That's a foundation, Marcus, even when it doesn't feel that way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Maybe. I'm not ready to get all optimistic or whatever. But I guess I don't feel quite as stuck as when I walked in. That's... yeah. That's something.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know that first step of walking through a door like this isn't always easy. What brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... I actually found some information online and it kind of clicked, you know? I just finished a detox program last week and I... I want to do this right. For my daughter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to do this right. For her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's four months old. And I just... I kept telling myself the wine was helping me cope, helping me sleep, helping me be a better mom somehow. But that's not — that's not really true, is it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What made you start to question that story you were telling yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: One night I was holding her and I realized I was counting down until I could put her to bed so I could have a glass. And I just — that's not the mom I want to be. That scared me more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment really shook something loose. The distance between who you were being and who you want to be for her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And now that I'm out of detox I'm just... honestly I'm terrified. Like, what if I can't handle the nights? What if the anxiety just comes back and I don't have anything to reach for? She still doesn't sleep through the night and I'm so exhausted and I just...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does that fear feel like — when you imagine one of those hard nights and there's nothing to reach for?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like falling with nothing to grab. I know that sounds dramatic but... my partner tries, he does, but he doesn't really get it. He sleeps through everything. And I'm up there at 2am alone with a screaming baby and I used to just think, okay, one more hour and I can have a glass and just... breathe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That was your lifeline. The thing that made the impossible feel just barely manageable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And now everyone keeps saying 'you did it, you're so strong' and I just... I don't feel strong. I feel like I traded one kind of exhaustion for another. Like, detox was hard and now recovery is going to be hard and I just want to know when does it get easier? When is there a break?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like there's no break in it. One hard thing right after another and people keep applauding you for it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. And I love her, I do — but I didn't expect it to feel like this. Nobody told me it would feel like this. The postpartum stuff, the not sleeping, just... losing yourself. I thought I'd be better at it. I thought I'd be a natural or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you that you're sitting here anyway — feeling all of that and still here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... I think about her growing up. And I think about my own mom, actually. She drank. Not a lot, but enough that I noticed. I swore I wouldn't be that. And then here I am and it's like — I became the exact thing I was afraid of. And it just snuck up on me so fast.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying something really heavy — the fear that you became something you swore you never would, and the grief of how fast it happened. And underneath all of that, there's still that little girl who noticed her mom.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I haven't really let myself think about that part. It hurts. She's going to remember things. Maybe not now, but someday. Kids notice everything. I noticed everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came here after detox — not because anyone made you, but because a single moment with your daughter made it undeniable. You're scared the hard nights will break you. You're exhausted and feel unseen. And underneath all of that there's something fierce and clear: you know exactly what it felt like to grow up with a parent who drank, and you will not let that be her story. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's all of it. I didn't expect to cry today. I thought I was past the crying part.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — even just a little bit — to be the mom you're picturing? Not perfect. Just different from what you're afraid of.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... present, I guess. Actually there. Not counting down or thinking about the next drink. Like, laughing at the stupid little faces she makes without that edge of just needing to get through it. I want to actually enjoy it. I feel like I've already missed so much and she's only four months old.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You haven't missed it. You're here fighting for it at four months. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I hope so. My partner said last night he was proud of me and I almost didn't believe him. It felt easier to just... believe the worst about myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's worth paying attention to. What would it take — even a little — to start believing what he sees?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just have to keep showing up. Small stuff. Get through tonight, get through tomorrow night. I actually made a list — things I can do when the urge hits. Tea, a bath, texting a friend. Stupid small stuff, but... maybe it helps.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That list isn't stupid. That's you building a survival kit out of what you actually have available to you. That's real work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, I guess it is. I keep waiting to feel ready, like some switch is gonna flip. But maybe this is what ready feels like. Scared but doing it anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to hold onto what you just said — scared but doing it anyway. You walked in here after finishing detox with a four-month-old at home, carrying this history you never asked for, and in the last hour you named exactly the kind of mother you want to be and the first steps you're already taking to get there. That's not nothing. That's everything.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thank you. I... yeah. I think I needed to hear that. I'll come back next week.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm glad you made it. Take whatever seat feels comfortable. So — before we get into anything formal — I'm just curious what today looks like from your side. What brought you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My buddy Ray basically wouldn't let up until I called. And then my doctor's got everyone all worked up over some bloodwork. I don't really — I mean, I'm here. But I want to be upfront, I don't think I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here, but it wasn't exactly your idea.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It was not. Look, I respect Ray, he means well, and I get that doctors gotta cover their ass — their bases. But a six-pack after work? I been doing that for fifteen years. It's not like I'm drinking in the morning or missing shifts or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got a system that works for you. And you're holding yourself to a real standard — showing up, doing the job. What exactly did your doctor tell you about the bloodwork?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Something about liver enzymes being elevated. AST, ALT — I don't know what any of that means. He's like, 'it could be serious.' Could be. Everything 'could be' something, right? I work construction, I breathe in God knows what every day. Could be that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a lot of possible explanations, and you're not ready to just accept that the drinking is the culprit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And I mean — look, I know six beers sounds like a lot to some people. But you talk to any guy on my crew, that's... that's Tuesday, you know? That's just what you do after a ten-hour pour in ninety-degree heat.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's woven into the whole culture of the job. Walk me through a normal day — like, what does it actually feel like when you get home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm beat. Like, physically wrecked. My back's been bad for years, knees are going. I get home, kids are doing their thing, wife's... we don't talk a lot anymore. So I sit on the porch, crack one open, and it's like — finally. You know? It's the only time my brain actually shuts up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That porch, that first beer — that's the one moment in the day that belongs to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And I'm not hurting anybody. I'm not — I'm not a mean drunk, I'm not driving around. I just... sit there. Maybe watch the game. I wake up, I go to work. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not causing chaos. That matters. Can I share something with you about what those enzyme numbers actually mean — just so you have the full picture? You can do whatever you want with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those enzymes — AST and ALT — they're basically signals that liver cells are under stress or breaking down. Elevated levels at your age, over time, can lead to scarring. The liver's actually pretty resilient early on, but once the scarring sets in, it doesn't reverse. Your doctor isn't crying wolf. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. I hear you. I just — I've been fine. I feel fine. Mostly. My back's the thing that gets me, not... not that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you is brushing it off. And another part — I'm watching your face right now — something landed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My dad. He had... he had liver issues. Cirrhosis, eventually. He died at sixty-two. I was twenty-six. I'm forty-two now and I... I don't think about that usually. I try not to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say. You've been carrying that a long time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to die like he did. He was... at the end he was yellow. Jaundice. Couldn't work. Couldn't do anything. That was — that's not how I want to go out. I got two kids.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your kids are in the picture when you think about this. What would it mean for them — and for you — if you made some kind of change here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it's... it feels big. Like I can't even picture it. The porch thing, that's — that's been my routine forever. But... I don't know. Maybe I've been telling myself it's fine because it's easier than dealing with the alternative.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing — tell me if I get it wrong. You're a guy who works incredibly hard, who's built his whole wind-down around that evening routine. You're not trying to cause problems, you're trying to get through the day. At the same time, you've got your doctor worried, you've got Ray worried, and now you're sitting here realizing that your dad's story might be closer to yours than you've wanted to admit. And underneath all of that, you've got two kids you want to be around for.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's about right. When you say it like that it sounds — I don't know. It sounds like I've been avoiding something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already done the hard part just by letting yourself see that. So I'm curious — not what you think you should do, not what Ray or your doctor wants — what feels like something you could actually imagine trying?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe cutting back. Like not stopping completely — I'm not ready for that and I'd be lying if I said I was. But maybe two, three instead of six. See what happens. See if I can even do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not making a promise you can't keep. You're being honest about where you are and giving yourself a real target. That's actually a solid place to start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's weird. I've never said any of this out loud before. The stuff about my dad, the... all of it. I came in here ready to argue with somebody and now I'm just — huh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing — walking in ready to fight and leaving with something that's actually yours. You've got a goal that came from you, not from Ray or your doctor. You know what's at stake, you know why it matters, and you know what you want to try first. What would help you actually follow through this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... keeping my dad in mind. When I reach for that fourth one. Think about him. I think that might actually work. It's worth trying anyway.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, before we get into anything — I know last week was a rough one for you. I want to make sure we're picking up in the right place. How are you doing coming in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... not great. It was a bad week. Really bad, actually. I don't even know where to start, like... yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something's sitting heavy on you today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. So — okay. After we talked last time I really did try. I told myself I wasn't gonna go out Thursday. And then Marcus texted and I just... I went anyway. And it turned into this whole thing and I didn't get back until like 4am and I had practice at 7. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happened at practice after that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Coach pulled me aside. Again. And he just... he didn't even yell. He just looked at me like he was done. Not angry, just — tired of me. And that was somehow way worse. I think he's actually gonna sit me. Like, permanently.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That look — the tiredness instead of the anger — that landed differently than anything he's said before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because when he's angry at least he still cares, right? When he's just... tired. I don't know. I just thought, what's the point anymore. I've been working toward this literally my whole life and I'm just throwing it away over stupid Thursday nights. It's pathetic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said you've been working toward this your whole life. I want to stay with that for a second — what does athletics mean to you, beyond just the sport itself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... everything? My dad played. My whole family, it's like — it's the one thing I've always been good at. It's not just something I do. It's like... who I am. Or was. I don't even know anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it's tied up in your identity — not just your performance, but who you are, what you carry from your family. And at the same time, when you go out with the guys... what does that give you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like I can just be normal for a second. Like, not the athlete, not the guy who has to be perfect 24/7. Just a 20-year-old. But then it... it blows up everything I actually care about so I don't even know why I keep doing it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There are two things you're describing that both feel real — the connection, the relief of just being a regular guy for a night... and the identity, the sport, what your dad passed down to you. And they keep colliding.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I never thought about it like that but... yeah. They do. All the time. And I never know which one I'm actually choosing when I'm in the moment.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've been hearing, because I think there's a lot here that's worth naming. You came in today after a hard week — you made an intention, Thursday came and it didn't hold, and now you're sitting with real fear about your spot on the team. Underneath that, though, I'm hearing two things that matter deeply to you: belonging with your teammates, and this sport that runs through your whole family. Does that feel like an accurate picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, that's pretty much it. I just didn't expect to feel this — I don't know. Like there's no version of this where I come out okay. Like I've already messed it up too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would 'okay' even look like for you, if you let yourself imagine it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... finishing the season. Actually starting again. Showing coach I'm not just talk. Getting back to where I was junior year — I was really playing well then. Like, genuinely. That felt good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just painted a really clear picture of what you want — finishing strong, rebuilding trust with your coach, getting back to that version of yourself. That's not nothing. That's a lot to care about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. It really is. I keep acting like it doesn't matter but — yeah. It does. It matters a lot actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned junior year specifically. What was different for you then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was just... focused. I wasn't really into the party stuff then. I had this whole routine — gym at 6am, meal prep on Sundays, it sounds so lame but I was locked in. My numbers were the best they'd ever been. Coach used to use me as an example in film sessions.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You built that — the 6am sessions, the routine, the results in film. That wasn't circumstance. That was you deciding what mattered and following through on it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — it wasn't easy, it was really hard actually. But yeah, I did do that. I did build that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thinking about this week coming up — what's one small thing that might look even slightly different, if you were moving toward that version of yourself again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... okay this might sound weird, but — talking to Marcus directly. He's my closest friend on the team, he genuinely doesn't care if I drink or not. I think I've just been using 'the guys' as an excuse when really it's me. Like if I just called him instead of showing up at the party... I don't know. Maybe that's too small.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not too small — that's you naming something real. There's a difference between the connection you actually want and the habit of going out, and you just identified it. Reaching out to Marcus is using your support system. That's how change actually starts, not in one big moment but in one phone call.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think I've been confusing those two things for a while. Like I thought I wanted one thing but I was actually just running from something else. That's... huh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've done real work today, especially coming in after a week like that. Before we wrap up — what's one thing you're leaving here with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That maybe I'm not as stuck as I thought I was. Like... it's not all gone. I still actually want to fix this. And I think — I think that matters. That I want to.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — I'm Sarah. Don't worry, I promise the couch is more comfortable than it looks. No agenda today, no paperwork to fill out right this second. So... what brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, yeah, hi. I'm Maya. So my doctor got some lab results back and they were... not great. She said my liver enzymes are elevated and that it's probably from drinking, and she kind of suggested I talk to someone. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like it landed pretty hard. What was going through your head when you got those results?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly I just kind of... stared at the email for like an hour. I've known for a while that I drink more than I should but seeing it in an actual medical document made it feel real in a different way. Like, it's not just a habit anymore, it's a thing that's showing up in my body.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's been this awareness sitting with you for a while — that the drinking was more than you wanted — and the lab results kind of forced it out into the open.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I know why I do it, that's the thing. I have really bad social anxiety and alcohol is just... it's the only way I can actually function at parties or work events or whatever. Sober me at a networking happy hour is a disaster. Drunk me can actually talk to people, make eye contact, seem like a normal human. I don't know how to be a person without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's actually really honest, and it makes complete sense — the drinking isn't random, it's been solving a real problem for you. What does it feel like when you try to picture showing up to those situations without it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrifying. Like I literally cannot picture it. I've tried a couple times — just showing up somewhere and not drinking — and I end up in a corner sweating, spiraling, and then I leave early. So it's not like I'm choosing alcohol over being normal. It's like alcohol is the reason I have any social life at all. If I stop... I probably just stop existing socially. That's not dramatic, that's just what happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Without it, you disappear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. I know that sounds... I don't know. But yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like anything except true for you right now. Can I ask — what does your social life actually look like day to day? Like outside of the events?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean I have friends. Sort of. I see them mostly at bars or parties. I don't really do sober hangouts. I get anxious even texting people sometimes — like I'll draft a message and delete it ten times before I just don't send it. So the people I actually talk to are mostly in situations where there's already going to be drinking, so I have a... reason to be okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So alcohol has kind of structured your whole social world — it's not just something you do at events, it's the thing that makes connection feel possible at all. And now you're sitting with these lab results and part of you knows something has to shift, but the cost feels enormous. Because it's not just cutting back on drinks — it's potentially losing the only version of yourself that can actually be in the room with other people.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God, when you say it like that... yeah. That's exactly it. And that's why this feels impossible. Like, I'm not going to choose my liver over having any kind of life. That sounds awful to say out loud but that's kind of where I'm at.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound awful. It sounds like someone who really cares about actually being in her own life — about connection, about being present. That want for real relationships, for not disappearing? That part of you is not the problem. That part's actually what's going to matter here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I want those things. I do. I just don't know how to get there without the thing that's been getting me there. That's the part I can't figure out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you if there was a path that didn't require that trade-off? I'm not saying there's a magic button — I'm asking what it would mean to you personally if one existed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it sounds nice in theory? But I've had anxiety my whole life and I've tried therapy before and it kind of didn't... I don't know. I left feeling like I'd talked a lot and nothing changed. So I guess I'm a little skeptical that there's some version of me that just gets fixed. Maybe I'm just wired this way and alcohol is just like, the workaround.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been fighting this for a long time and what you tried didn't get you where you needed to go — so hope feels risky. Like if you let yourself believe in something and it doesn't work, that's its own kind of loss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. That's actually scarier than just staying where I am. At least where I am I know what I'm dealing with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes complete sense. And I want to be straight with you — I'm not going to promise a fix. But I will say this, and you can take it for whatever it's worth: social anxiety and alcohol use together is one of the most common and most studied combinations we see. There's actually specific treatment built for exactly this, not generic 'drink less' advice, but stuff that addresses the anxiety underneath. You're not uniquely broken. You found a solution to a real problem with the tools that were available to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't know it was like... a recognized thing. That they go together. I kind of just assumed I was weak and this was a me problem. A character flaw or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it do for you to know that it's not weakness — that there's an actual neurological and psychological reason this developed the way it did?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... that would be kind of a relief, honestly. I've spent a long time being angry at myself for not being able to just white-knuckle through it and be normal. If there's actually a reason it happened... I don't know. Maybe I'd be less afraid to try something different. Maybe it would feel less like I'm just fighting my own personality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here saying this feels impossible, and you just said 'maybe I'd be less afraid to try.' That's not nothing. That's actually kind of a big deal, and you did that in like forty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. I guess. I mean I still don't know what 'trying something' would look like in real life. Like my company holiday party is in six weeks and the thought of going sober is still... a lot. That feels like a very concrete problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay so here's where you've landed today — you came in with scary lab results, and underneath that there's this whole picture: anxiety that's been running the show for years, alcohol that solved a real problem but is now creating a new one, a lot of fear about what change might cost you socially. And also this: you're still here talking, you didn't shut down, and something in you cracked open just a little to the idea that there might be another way. That's a lot for a walk-in appointment on a Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I didn't expect to actually talk about any of this. I thought you'd just like... hand me a pamphlet and tell me to cut back to two drinks. This was different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No pamphlets, I promise. So — what feels like a possible next step? Even a small one. Doesn't have to be the holiday party.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... maybe coming back? Like, actually scheduling a real appointment. I don't think I've done therapy that felt like it was actually about the real thing before. This felt like the real thing.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Welcome, come on in. I'm glad you reached out. Before we get into anything, I just want you to know this is a completely judgment-free space — whatever you share stays here. So, what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I saw something online and I just — I don't know. I've been thinking about my drinking for a while and I finally just made myself come in. Which I'm already kind of regretting, honestly. Like sitting in the parking lot I almost left.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you almost didn't make it through the door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — I want to be clear, I'm not like... I'm not an alcoholic or whatever. I just use it to get through social stuff. Every party, every work happy hour, every date. I cannot do any of it without drinking first. Which sounds bad when I say it out loud but it's just how it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about what it looks like — getting through those situations.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get so in my head. Like I'll be standing at a party and I'm convinced everyone thinks I'm boring or weird and without a drink I just... freeze. My brain goes completely blank and I want to disappear. So I drink. And it just takes the edge off and suddenly I can actually, like, form sentences. Talk to people. It works, you know? That's the thing. It works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So alcohol has become a really important tool for you. It's the thing that lets you actually show up and function in situations that feel genuinely overwhelming without it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right, exactly. So why would I even want to stop? Like — I know that sounds... ugh. I don't know why I'm here. I don't know what I'm expecting you to do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something brought you here though. What was it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My friend made this comment at a party last month. She said, "oh, Maya never goes anywhere without a drink in her hand," and she was laughing like it was a joke, but it just... stuck. And then I started actually paying attention and I was like, oh. That's true. I'm always the first one at the bar. Always. I don't even really think about it, I just do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That comment landed differently than you expected.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It was embarrassing. Like I've always known I do this — I'm not oblivious — but hearing someone else say it out loud was different. It made me feel like... I'm not as in control as I tell myself I am? That bothered me. It really bothered me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does being in control look like to you, when it comes to this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I want it to feel like a choice. Right now it doesn't feel like a choice, it feels like I *have* to or I'm going to humiliate myself. And that's — that bothers me. But I also genuinely don't know how I'd function at like a work networking thing without it. My job has a lot of that and I'm terrible at it sober. Genuinely terrible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm hearing you right. You came in because what your friend said made something click — and you realized this feels less like a choice and more like something you have to do. You're not necessarily saying you want to stop altogether. But that lack of control, that feeling of having to — that's what's sitting with you. Does that fit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's actually it. I don't want to become someone who can't go to a party at all. I just don't want to be the person who needs three drinks before she can even say hi to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it look like — if things were different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think about it sometimes. Like, going to a work thing and just being... normal. Having one drink or even none and being able to actually talk to people without my heart pounding. I don't know if that's even possible for me though. My anxiety is really bad. Like, clinically bad. I was diagnosed in college.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The anxiety feels like the thing underneath all of this — and part of what's scary about changing anything is the question of what you'd even have left to manage it with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like what do I do then, just... be anxious all the time? At least right now I have something that actually works. Taking that away feels — it feels really scary. I don't know what I'd look like without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes a lot of sense. Can I ask — have you ever tried managing the social anxiety in any other way? Even something small, even briefly?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I mean, I used to do breathing stuff. In college I had a therapist for a bit and she taught me some techniques. I kind of stopped. I think because it never felt as... reliable? Like alcohol works every time without fail. The breathing stuff was more hit or miss. So I just... drifted away from it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've actually done this work before. You learned real strategies, you practiced them — and they helped, at least some of the time. That tells me something important: the anxiety isn't something you've never dealt with. You've been actively managing it for years. Just in a way that's starting to cost you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I never thought about it that way. I always frame it as like, I'm weak because I can't just be normal. But I guess I have been dealing with it, just... not well. That's a weirdly less terrible way to see it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you — personally — to find a way through the anxiety that you actually felt good about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. It would be huge. Like, I'd feel like I actually had my life together. Right now I'm just barely keeping it together, you know? I can hide at work because it's coding, it's mostly just me and my laptop. But socially I'm just... treading water. If I could go to a party and actually be okay without needing a drink first... I don't know. I'd feel like a real person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard today. You came in because a comment from your friend made something click — you've known for a while that alcohol has shifted from something you enjoy to something you feel you need. Underneath all of it is real, diagnosed anxiety that you've been managing for years, mostly alone. You're not sure you want to stop drinking entirely, but you want to feel like you have a choice — like you're deciding rather than depending. And when you imagine actually having tools that work, something in you lights up a little. That about right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... when you put it like that it sounds less like I'm broken and more like I just haven't figured this out yet. Which is... I don't know. That's a different feeling than I walked in with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Exactly. So if we were to think about one small step — just one thing you might want to try or notice between now and next time — what feels even a little bit possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... maybe I try that breathing stuff again. Like, at one event. Just see what happens — I'm not promising anything. But maybe that. And, um... I think I actually want to come back. Which is not what I expected to say when I walked in here.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. Grab a seat wherever feels right — fair warning, the couch looks comfortable but it's a trap. I'm Marcus. So, your sister mentioned you just finished up a detox program. How you holding up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Yeah. Okay, I guess? It's just... it's weird being out. Like everything feels kind of loud again. I don't — I don't really know why I'm here, to be honest. My sister set this whole thing up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does 'weird' feel like for you right now — like, what's going through your head sitting in this room?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Like I'm in trouble. Like I got sent to the principal's office. Which is kind of dumb because I'm literally 27.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know you're an adult, you chose to walk through that door — and it still feels like someone's about to hand you a detention slip.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah, kind of. I just... I've never done anything like this before. I always figured, like, I work in a bar. Everybody drinks. It's just — it's part of the job, you know? That's how I always looked at it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years behind a bar, right? So you've basically been marinating in that world since you were what, 24. What was it that actually made you go through with the detox — something must've shifted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, three years. And uh... my sister. She asked me something and I couldn't answer it. She asked when the last day was that I didn't drink. And I just — I stood there. Nothing came up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real honesty, man. A lot of people would've just invented an answer on the spot. You actually sat with the question instead of faking your way past it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I mean, I still don't know. I actually went back later and tried to think of a day. Any day. And I couldn't find one. Not in like a year at least.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you did some searching on your own after she asked. What was that like, going back through and looking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uncomfortable. Like, I'd think oh — that weekend trip, and then no, we had a cooler. Or Christmas, and no... yeah no. Every time I thought I had one it didn't hold up. At some point I just stopped looking because it was starting to freak me out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It started feeling like the answer wasn't there. And that scared you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, I'm a bartender. I'm not like... I always thought of alcoholics as, like, a different kind of person. You know? But that math I was doing didn't feel like normal-person math.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it bring up for you — sitting with the idea that it might not just be 'bartender stuff'?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... scary. Like if it's not just the job, then what is it? And then — then what do I do? That bar is my whole social life. My coworkers, my regulars, I'd call half of them friends. If I'm not drinking with them I'm just... I don't know what I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're not just worried about the drinking. You're worried about losing your whole world.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Basically, yeah. Is that — is that stupid? It sounds stupid saying it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Doesn't sound stupid at all. Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing — you came out of detox, this session wasn't really your idea, but your sister asked one question and you couldn't shake it. You went looking for a sober day and came up empty. And now you're sitting here not just scared about the drinking itself, but about whether there's a version of your life that still makes sense without alcohol in it. That about right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's a lot, but. Yeah. That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's what I want to ask — take your time with this — what would need to be true for you to believe that version of your life is possible?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... maybe if I could still be around those people without it being weird. Like if I could still show up, pour drinks, and not feel like I'm missing out or like everyone's looking at me different. Like I'm less than or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just described something really specific. You're not saying 'I want to be normal' in some vague way — you're saying you want to keep your people, keep your job, and still feel like yourself. That's not wishful thinking. That's an actual thing to work toward.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it like that. It always felt like... like it's one or the other. Give everything up or nothing changes. I didn't see a middle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — like who you are as a person — if things did start to shift? Not just the drinking. The bigger picture.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd feel like I had my head back. Like I wake up some mornings and it's just... fog. And I've started not trusting my own memory on stuff. Little things. And I hate that. I used to be sharp. I want to be sharp again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a version of you that you remember. Clear-headed, on top of things. And part of you is grieving not being that guy right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I think so. I didn't expect to say that out loud but. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've said more out loud today than I think you thought you would coming in here. What feels most important to hold onto from this conversation — something you want to carry with you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That it's not one or the other. And that... I actually want to feel sharp again. I think that's the first time I've let myself say that. Even to myself.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Marcus — most people drop the 'doctor' part pretty fast, makes the whole thing feel less like a root canal. Can I grab you some water? And, uh — what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, no, I'm okay, thanks. I, uh... my advisor kind of sent me here. Or — strongly suggested. Which, with her, is basically the same thing. I honestly don't really know what to expect.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this wasn't exactly your idea — she nudged you through the door. And you still came. That actually takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. I've been — things have been harder than I've been letting on. To anyone, really. The thesis, the whole program... it's just a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say it's 'a lot' — what does that actually look like for you, day to day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... I wake up already behind. I work until 2am most nights trying to catch up. And I've been drinking more than I should — I know that, I'm not an idiot — but it helps me sleep, takes the edge off the anxiety. I just can't, like... I don't know, stop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking's been doing something real for you — getting you through nights that feel impossible. And I'm hearing a 'but' in there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Big but. My advisor pulled me aside last week and said my last two chapters were... not good. And she has been really patient with me, so if she's actually saying something out loud, I know it's bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like, hearing it from her specifically?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was like... confirmation. Of everything I already think about myself. Like, maybe I just don't belong there. I got into the program and they made a mistake. Everyone around me is just — genuinely brilliant — and I'm just... pretending. I've always been pretending.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feeling of waiting to be found out. Like any day someone's going to look up and go, 'wait, how did he get in here?'

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And the drinking makes it worse — I'm not stupid, I know that. I have a few drinks, feel okay for a minute, wake up feeling like garbage, can't write anything, feel like a total fraud, drink again to cope with feeling like a fraud... it's this whole loop. And I don't — I don't see how it changes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just mapped out the whole loop really clearly — from inside it. That's actually harder than it sounds. So what made today different? Why come in at all?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My advisor... she said she believed in me. Which I don't — I don't really know what to do with that. But she's not someone who says things she doesn't mean. She doesn't do the empty encouragement thing. So... I don't know. Some part of me wanted to try. Even if I don't really believe it yet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So underneath all of this, there's a part of you that hasn't completely given up. And that part is the one that walked through the door today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I used to care so much about this work. Like, genuinely care. When I got in I was so excited, I called my parents, I — ... now I just feel numb most of the time. And tired. Really tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the research itself — what are you actually working on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Machine learning applications in early cancer detection. Which — like, it matters. It genuinely matters. I just... somewhere in the last year I stopped feeling that. Now it just feels like this thing that's going to expose me as someone who can't actually do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That work is real. And for just a second when you described it — your voice actually changed a little. I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Did it? I didn't notice. I mean... yeah. I do care about it. I think I've been so stuck in my head that I can't access it anymore. The drinking numbs everything — the anxiety, sure — but also the good stuff. The part of me that actually wants to be there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together, make sure I'm getting it right. You came into this program with real passion — cancer detection, work that actually means something to you. The pressure piled up, the imposter syndrome got loud, and drinking became the way to get through it. It takes the edge off, but it's also been cutting you off from the part of you that loves the work. And now your advisor's noticing, you're noticing, but you feel like you're inside a loop with no exit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... hearing it like that is kind of a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Kind of a lot how?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Heavy. But also... accurate? Like, you're not telling me anything I don't already know. I just haven't — I've never said it out loud before. To someone who wasn't going to freak out or start treating me differently.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you think about the version of you who called his parents when he got into the program — the guy who was actually excited about that research — what would he want to do with everything we've talked about today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He'd want to actually fix it. Not just white-knuckle through the next chapter. Like, actually address the thing instead of just... numbing it until the degree is done and then figuring it out after.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That guy isn't as far away as you think. He actually showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I mean... okay, so what does this actually look like? Like — do I need rehab? Is that where this is going? Because I don't know if I'm ready for that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a decision we'd make right now, and it's definitely not one I'd make for you — we'd figure out what the right support looks like together, based on what actually fits your life. But before we get there, I want to ask you something. If you had to pick just one small thing — one thing you'd be willing to try this week that might start to crack that loop open a little — what would it be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... not drinking the night before I have to write. That's when it's worst — I wake up and my brain just won't start and then the whole day is gone. I don't know if I can do it every time but... maybe I could try it once. See what happens.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this isn't exactly how you'd choose to spend your afternoon. Before we get into anything, I just want to say — this is your time, there's no agenda I'm trying to push. So... what would be most helpful to start with?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm here because the judge said I had to be. That's it. I don't... I mean, I've got nothing against you personally, but I don't think I need to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. The court sent you, and you're showing up — even if part of you would rather be anywhere else. That actually takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... sure. Look, I made a mistake. I drove when I probably shouldn't have. But I wasn't — I wasn't stumbling around or anything. I just... it was a bad night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A bad night. Tell me a little more about that — what was going on for you that night?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... my daughter's birthday. First one since the divorce finalized. I wasn't invited to the party. My ex had her whole new... whatever going on, and I just — I sat in my apartment and I drank. And then I shouldn't have gotten in the car. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You missed your daughter's birthday. And you were alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. She's nine. Nine years old and I'm not there. That's... I don't know. It is what it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I notice you started to say something and then pulled back — "that's..." What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. It's hard. I don't really... I'm not used to talking about this stuff. My ex used to say I never talked about anything. Maybe she had a point, I guess. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like the divorce really turned your world upside down. How has the drinking fit into all of that — these last four months?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... it helps me not think. I get home from work and the apartment is quiet and I just — I can't stand it. Before, there was noise. Kids running around, dinner, all of it. Now there's just... nothing. So yeah, I drink. It makes the evenings shorter.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking gives you some relief from how quiet and empty things feel now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I know it sounds pathetic. A 48-year-old man who can't handle being alone. But I was married for nineteen years. Nineteen. That's more than half my adult life. And now it's just... gone. She's gone, the house is gone, and I only see my kids every other weekend.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nineteen years. That's not just a marriage — that's most of who you were day to day. What's that been like, trying to figure out who you are now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't know how to do it. I don't... I don't know who I am without all that. I wake up on a Saturday and there's nowhere I need to be and that used to sound amazing, you know? And now it's just... I don't know what to do with it. I feel like everything that mattered is just... it's done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Everything that gave your life structure and meaning — it all came through that family, that home. And right now, without it, things feel pretty empty. Maybe even pointless.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean — yeah. I'm not going to do anything stupid, if that's what you're asking. I'm not there. But, um... there are mornings where I wake up and I just don't see what the next ten years looks like. Like, what am I actually working toward?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for being honest about that. That took courage to say.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't said that out loud before. I don't even... my brother keeps telling me to man up, get back out there, you know. Nobody wants to hear that you're lost.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been carrying this alone. And the drinking has been the one thing that makes it bearable enough to get through the night. I'm curious — when you imagine things being different a year from now, what would you want that to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be a good dad. That's... honestly, that's the one thing I keep coming back to. My kids are ten and nine. They still need me. And I'm worried that if I keep going the way I'm going I'm gonna — I don't know. Mess that up too.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being a good dad — that still matters deeply to you. Even in the middle of all this loss, that's still there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I mean... I've screwed up a lot the last few months. The DUI, just — the way I've been living. But those kids didn't do anything wrong. They shouldn't have to lose their dad too just because... just because things fell apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You came in here today because the court said you had to — and honestly, part of you was ready to just go through the motions. But underneath that, there's a man who's been blindsided by loss. Nineteen years of a life, gone in four months. You've been drinking to get through the nights because the silence is unbearable. And at the same time, there's something you haven't lost — being a father. And that's what you're afraid of losing next.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's pretty much it. I didn't expect to actually — I thought I'd just sit here and answer some questions and leave. I didn't think I'd actually say any of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted for you today. What do you think you'd be willing to consider — even just a small step — when it comes to the drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I can just stop. I'm not ready to say that. But maybe... maybe I could try talking to someone. Like this. More than once. Because I think — I think I've been doing a lot of damage just by keeping all this inside.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here skeptical, and you're leaving with something — a small opening. That's not nothing. The fact that you can still name what matters to you, that you're thinking about your kids — that's something real to build on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, maybe. I'm not — I'm not going to pretend I've got it figured out. But... I'll come back. I think I need to come back.

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Jamie. Coffee's over there if you want it — fair warning, it's terrible, but it's free, so, you know, trade-offs. Go ahead and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. Look, I'm just going to say upfront — I don't really want to be here. My lawyer said I had to do this, so I'm doing it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, that tracks. Honestly, most people who walk through that door didn't exactly pencil this in on their vision board. So you're here because a judge said so — that's a pretty lousy reason to spend a Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And I've done the therapy thing before, so — no offense — but I kind of know how this goes. You're going to tell me I have a problem, I'm going to push back, we're going to go in circles for however many sessions the court requires, and then I'm done. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hm. So you've got the whole thing mapped out already. What was it like, those other times — the going in circles part?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was a waste of time. They just kept pushing this narrative that I'm like... some kind of alcoholic, which is — that's not me. I have a stressful job, I like to unwind, I'm 28. That's just... that's what people do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You felt like they had you in a box before you even opened your mouth.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's exactly it. Like, I work in marketing, I'm good at my job, I have my life together. One bad night doesn't make me — it doesn't define me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've worked really hard to build something you're proud of. That comes through. And yeah — one night isn't a person's whole story. I'm not here to slap a label on you. I'm just... curious about you, honestly. What actually happened that night, in your words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was a work event. Open bar, which, you know — everyone was drinking. I had more than I should have, I'll admit that. I thought I was okay to drive, I wasn't, and I got pulled over. It's — look, it was a mistake. A really expensive, embarrassing mistake, but it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word — embarrassing — you said it pretty quickly. What's the embarrassing part for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm supposed to be the one who has it together, you know? My team looks up to me. And now there's a mugshot, apparently, which — great. That's just great. My mom found out and she's been calling every day and it's just... it's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So underneath the anger at being here, there's also just... a lot of fallout you're dealing with. Your image at work, your mom, the legal stuff. That's genuinely a heavy load to be carrying around.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah. Yeah, it is. I haven't really... I don't know, I haven't slept well since it happened. Keep replaying it. Like what if something had happened, what if I'd — yeah. I don't want to think about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That replay — it sounds like part of you knows it could've gone a lot worse.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Obviously. I'm not an idiot. I know I got lucky. That doesn't mean I have a — it doesn't mean this is a pattern or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding two things at once right now — 'I got lucky' and 'but this isn't a pattern.' I'm not going to argue either of those. What I'm wondering is, when you say after-work drinks or events with open bars... how often are we actually talking about?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like... probably three, four nights a week? But that's just — that's the industry. Marketing is very social. Client dinners, happy hours, launch parties. It's part of the job, it's not like I'm sitting alone drinking a bottle of wine by myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So most of it is social, tied to work. And on those nights — what does drinking actually do for you? Like what's the payoff?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It just... turns the volume down, I guess. Like I can stop performing. I'm 'on' all day — emails, presentations, managing people — and after a few drinks I can just... be a person for a minute. Is that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Turning the volume down. That's a really honest thing to say, and it makes a lot of sense given how much pressure you're describing. I'm curious — are there other ways you've found to get that same relief, or has it pretty much always been this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to run. Like, a lot, in college. I don't really do that anymore. I keep saying I will. I don't know, somewhere along the way everything just got... I got busier and it kind of fell away.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something that actually worked for you — and it got crowded out. The version of you that ran — what was she like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She was... less anxious, I think. Like I handled stuff better. I didn't need — I mean, I still drank in college, but it wasn't the same. It didn't feel like I needed it. Hm. I haven't thought about that in a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you've actually said a lot today without maybe realizing it. You came in pretty sure this was going to be a waste of time — and I respect that, honestly. But you also told me you haven't been sleeping, you're replaying that night, you know it could've been worse. You described drinking as the main way you turn the volume down now, when it didn't used to be that way. And there's a version of you — the runner — who had other tools. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that it sounds... I don't know. I guess I've been telling myself this is all fine and normal and maybe I... I don't know. Maybe I haven't been totally honest with myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes guts to say. Seriously. What would 'being more honest with yourself' look like, if you let yourself go there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think it would mean admitting that the DUI wasn't actually that surprising. Like... deep down. I've driven home like that before and just gotten away with it. And that's — okay that one's hard to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there? That's the most important thing anyone's said in this room all week. And I mean that. You didn't have to go there, and you did. I don't want to push too hard on our first day — but I do want to ask: given everything you just said, is there any part of you that's open to looking at this differently than you have before?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Maybe. I mean, I'm still not — I don't want to make this into some huge dramatic thing. But maybe, yeah. Maybe a small part of me is tired of just managing it, you know?

client_context: A 28-year-old marketing professional who drinks heavily at social events and after work. Recently got a DUI. Feels embarrassed but insists it was a one-time mistake.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know you mentioned you're squeezed for time today, so I want to make sure we use it well. Before I say anything else — can you tell me, in your own words, what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... the court said I had to be here, so. That's pretty much it. I got a DUI, which — okay, yes, that happened, but it was one night. One. I'm not like, an alcoholic or whatever. I just want to be clear about that upfront.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here because it's required — and you want to make sure I understand this feels like an isolated incident, not some kind of pattern.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. I work in marketing, I go to client dinners, happy hours — that's literally part of my job. Everyone in my industry drinks like that. I just... happened to get caught on a bad night. It doesn't mean anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it been like — since that night? The whole process, the court dates, everything that came after?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Humiliating. I had to call my parents. I had to tell my manager I needed time off for court dates without fully explaining why at first. My license is suspended so I'm taking Ubers everywhere like... it's been a nightmare. But that's all just — that's the legal fallout, not like a drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's been really embarrassing — having to tell the people who matter to you what happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Especially my mom. She didn't — she didn't yell or anything, but I could just tell she was waiting for me to fall apart. And I'm not falling apart. I'm fine. I made a mistake, I'm dealing with the consequences, and that should be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying a lot — keeping it together for everyone, reassuring them. What do you think your mom saw that had her worried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. Maybe just — okay, the past few months have been stressful. We had a restructuring at work, I took on this huge new account, and I was drinking after work more than usual. Like, more than I normally would. But that's situational. That's stress management.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You noticed it yourself — that the amount had shifted. That kind of self-awareness isn't nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I did notice. I mean, I wasn't blacking out or missing work or anything. But there were nights — Tuesdays, Wednesdays — where I'd finish my third glass of wine and think, okay, that was probably too much. And then the next week gets crazy and you just... keep going.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those moments where you thought 'that was too much' — what was that like for you, sitting with that thought?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... pushed it aside. You tell yourself you're busy, it's a demanding industry, this is just what it looks like right now. But sometimes I'd wake up the next morning and feel — not just hungover, like actually ashamed. That's different. I don't love that feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That shame stayed with you even after the week moved on and things got busy again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I hate it. I — I have goals, you know? I want to make director by the time I'm thirty. I want to actually have a life outside of work at some point. And then you have a week where you're just numbing out every single night and it's like... that's not who I want to be. That's not the person I pictured.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this version of yourself you're working toward — driven, building something real — and drinking has started to feel like it's pulling you away from her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Kind of. I hadn't put it that way but yeah. And the DUI made it really hard to keep ignoring. Like I can't just say it's fine. My license is gone, I have community service hours, there are real consequences now. It's in my face.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just check in with you, because you've shared a lot in a short amount of time. You came in saying this was a one-time mistake — and I hear that, you don't want to be labeled. And you've also told me you noticed yourself drinking more under stress, that there were mornings with real shame, and that the DUI is making it hard to keep telling yourself everything is fine. Does that feel like an accurate picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's — yeah. I mean, I still don't think I'm an alcoholic. I want to be really clear on that. But I guess I've been using it more than I should. More than I want to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would your life look like if drinking wasn't something you had to manage or keep an eye on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd just feel... cleaner? More in control. I'd probably sleep better. And I wouldn't spend Sunday mornings running the mental math on whether I overdid it the night before. That actually sounds — that sounds kind of really nice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That picture — feeling cleaner, more in control, not running those numbers in your head — that clearly matters to you. You haven't stopped caring about who you want to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just got so used to the way things are that I forgot what it felt like before. Like, a year ago I was going to the gym on weekday mornings. I haven't done that in forever. I miss that version of my life, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're reconnecting with a version of yourself you actually want to get back to. If you were going to take one small step this week — not a huge overhaul, just one thing — what might that be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe just... not drinking on weeknights if there's no work event. Like, if I'm just home, just — skip it. That feels doable. I don't know if I'll manage it every night, but it feels way more realistic than 'stop drinking forever,' which just makes me want to shut down.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really thoughtful place to start — you're not setting yourself up to fail, you're giving yourself something concrete to try. And just noticing what makes you want to pour that glass on a random Tuesday? That information is going to tell you a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think so too. And I — I actually feel a little better having said all of this out loud. I've been holding it pretty tight. Like, I didn't want anyone to think I had a problem because then that makes it real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today because you had to — not exactly by choice — and you were honest anyway. You said things out loud that you haven't said to anyone. That takes real courage.
