You've got a clear sense of the person you want to be, a small concrete step to try, and you're not pretending anymore that everything is fine. That's a genuinely good place to end today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thanks. I, um... yeah. I think I might actually come back. Like, on my own. Not just because the court says I have to.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi Sarah. I'm really glad you made it today. I know getting time to yourself — even just for a call — can feel like a whole thing when you've got kids in the house. How are you doing right now, just... in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um. I'm okay. The kids are with my mom so it's actually quiet for once, which is — yeah. It's fine. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'quiet for once' — what's it usually like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... loud. Chaotic. My daughter's twelve and my son just turned nine and they fight constantly, and I'm working full-time, and there's just... there's always something, you know? There's always some fire to put out. I don't really get a break. But that's just — that's just what it is. Single mom life, right? I knew what I was signing up for.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew what you were signing up for... and you're carrying all of it, every day, mostly alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yeah. But plenty of people do it. My mom did it. It's not like I'm special or anything. I just... I handle it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And part of how you handle it — can you tell me a little about that? What does the end of your day usually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Kids go to bed around nine, nine-thirty. And then I just... sit. Pour a glass of wine. Watch something on my laptop or just sit in the quiet for a while. It's like — it's the only time all day that's mine, you know? And the wine kind of helps me decompress. I know that's probably why I'm here but it's not like I'm, like, drunk or anything. I'm functional. I go to work, I take care of my kids.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That time after nine o'clock — it sounds like it's sacred to you. The only moment in the whole day where you exist just for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's actually exactly it. Sacred. I never thought of it like that but — yeah. And I'm not hurting anyone. I'm not driving anywhere, the kids are asleep. I just sit there and I finally breathe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You figured out a way to give yourself something, even inside a life that doesn't leave much room for that. That's not nothing, Sarah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean... I don't know. I've been thinking lately that maybe it's — it started as like one glass and now it's just kind of... the whole bottle. Most nights. And I wake up and I feel okay, mostly, but there's this kind of... I don't know. Heaviness. I don't know if that's the wine or just life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not sure whether to blame the wine or just... everything else you're carrying. What does that heaviness feel like in the morning?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... foggy, kind of. Not sick, just — foggy. And my daughter, she's sharp, she notices things. She made a comment a few weeks ago, she was like, 'Mom, are you tired again?' And I just — I snapped at her. And then I felt horrible. Because she wasn't wrong. I was tired. But I was also... I don't know. I felt caught, I guess. By a twelve-year-old.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
...

Your daughter saw you. And something about that hurt.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. Because I've worked so hard to make sure they don't — I don't want them to worry about me. That's not their job. And when she said that I just... I remember thinking, like, is this what she sees? Is this who I am to her?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That question you asked yourself — 'is this who I am to her?' — what comes up for you when you sit with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I don't want to be someone she has to take care of someday. My mom had her own stuff and I spent a lot of years... I just swore I wouldn't do that to my kids. And I don't think I'm there, like I said I'm functional, but I also know that bottle of wine didn't used to be a bottle. It used to be a glass and a half and I talked myself into more and more and I kind of just... stopped asking myself why.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You stopped asking yourself why. And right now, sitting here — what do you think the answer might be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I'm... I'm tired in a way that sleep doesn't fix. I'm lonely. I love my kids more than anything, but God, I am so lonely. And there's no one — there's no one to call at ten o'clock at night when everything's quiet and I'm still wound up from the day. So I just... pour the wine and I sit with it and it does something. It takes the edge off. And I know that's not — I know that's not a solution.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just said something really brave. The loneliness, the tiredness that goes bone-deep — and you still know it's not a solution. Both of those things are true at the same time, and you're holding both of them right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never actually said that out loud before. The lonely part. It's embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's not embarrassing. It's human. And I wonder — if the wine weren't there at ten o'clock, what do you think you'd actually need in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think I'd need someone to just... talk to. Not about the kids or work or money stuff. Just — I don't know. Something that's just mine. Maybe a friend. Maybe just to feel like I exist as a person and not just a, a function. A mom-function.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A person, not just a function. You want to exist for yourself again, not just for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I think — I think that's why I haven't wanted to look at the drinking too hard, because if I take that away and there's nothing to replace it, then I'm just sitting there at ten o'clock with all of that. With the loneliness. And that sounds... that sounds terrible. But I also think maybe I've been avoiding it for too long. I can feel it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I've been hearing, and you can tell me if I'm getting it right. You're someone who has been holding up an enormous amount — full-time work, two kids, doing it alone — and somewhere along the way the wine became the one thing that was just yours, the thing that helped you breathe. And you've started to see it differently, not because someone told you to, but because of your daughter's face, and because you know yourself. You know it's crept from a glass to a bottle. You know it leaves a fog. And underneath all of it there's a loneliness you haven't really let yourself name before today. And what I'm hearing — underneath the part that's scared — is that you actually really want something more than just getting through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. Yeah, that's — you got it. That's it exactly. I didn't think I'd cry today, I was ready to be defensive about it and explain myself but that's — yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in ready to defend yourself and instead you just told me the truth about your loneliness. That took something real. So I want to ask you — not what you think you should do, but what feels like one small thing, something that's actually possible given your life — what might feel like a first step toward that person you want to exist as again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... maybe not starting with the whole bottle. Like, just — one glass and then see what happens. See if I can sit with the quiet without needing more of it. And maybe actually text my friend Diane back. I've been ghosting her for like three months because I didn't have the energy to explain anything. But maybe I don't have to explain everything. Maybe I just say hey.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. Take a seat wherever feels comfortable. I appreciate you coming in — I know first sessions can feel a little strange. What brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Yeah, so... my doctor called a few weeks back. Said some of my lab results came back off. Liver stuff. And she kind of strongly suggested I talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Getting a call like that out of the blue — what was that like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I kind of laughed it off at first. Like, I'm 27, you know? People my age don't have liver problems. But then it just... it kept sitting there in the back of my head. Wouldn't really go away.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It wouldn't let you just move on and forget about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And then she mentioned the liver numbers specifically, and I know — I mean, I know why they're off. I'm not stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Say more about that — what do you think is driving those numbers?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm a bartender. I drink after every shift. It's like... that's just what you do in the industry, right? Everyone does it. It's how you decompress after a long night. But I was sitting there the other day trying to think of the last time I didn't drink and I couldn't. Like, actually couldn't come up with one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've woven it so deep into your routine that there's no clear line anymore between unwinding and just... needing it to get through.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I'd say needing. I don't really like that word. But... yeah. Maybe. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to admit. A lot of people would've stopped at 'it's just the industry' and left it there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it is the industry. But I'm not an idiot. I know something's off. I just don't know what to do about it. Or if I even can do anything about it at this point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Walk me through what a typical day looks like for you right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Wake up late 'cause I work nights. Feel like garbage. Coffee. Maybe eat something. Go in, work a seven or eight hour shift, get off around two in the morning, have a few drinks with the other staff — it's social, you know, it's not like I'm drinking alone in some corner. Then go home and crash. That's it. Every day. Same thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wake up feeling rough, push through a long shift, close out the night with drinks, sleep, and repeat. That's a heavy cycle to be living inside of.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm tired all the time. Like... bone tired. And I keep telling myself that's just adulting, or whatever. Long hours, late nights. But maybe that's not all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you weren't drinking every day — what do you imagine might be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Huh. I don't know, I've never really... I think I'd feel things more? Like I'm kind of numb a lot of the time and I've been telling myself that's just how I am, that's just my personality. But I wasn't always like this. I used to actually care about stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to be straight with you about something. Those elevated liver enzymes your doctor flagged — they're a sign your liver is working a lot harder than it should be. It's not a death sentence, but it is your body sending up a flare. And the fact that you're here means some part of you is listening to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I knew that. I mean, I kind of knew that. It's different when someone actually says it out loud though. ...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What matters most to you? If you close your eyes and think about five years from now — what do you actually want your life to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My sister. She's nineteen and she, like, actually looks up to me and I don't know why. I don't want her to see me fall apart. And I had this thing with music — I used to produce stuff in my room, I was actually decent at it. Haven't touched it in like two years. I keep saying I'll get back to it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together for a second. You came in because your body gave you a warning you couldn't keep ignoring. And as we've been talking, it sounds like there's a version of you underneath all of this — someone who cares deeply about his sister, who used to make music, who's exhausted and a little numb, and who's maybe scared about where things are heading if nothing changes. That's a lot to be carrying around quietly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. When you say it like that I feel kind of stupid for not seeing it sooner.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would a first step even look like for you? Not the whole mountain — just one thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... cutting back? Like not every single night. I'm not — I don't think I can just stop cold, that honestly kind of scares me. But maybe like, not every night. Give myself a night off here and there and see how it feels.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're being really honest about what actually feels possible right now, instead of just telling me what you think I want to hear. That's not nothing — that's exactly the kind of honesty that makes change actually stick.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never said any of this out loud before. Not to anyone. It's... weird. It's kind of a relief? But also kind of terrifying.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: As we wrap up today — what do you want to take with you from this conversation?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That... maybe this doesn't have to just be my whole life. Like, I came in thinking I was here to check a box because my doctor told me to. But I don't know. Maybe this is actually about something.
